items.html:
Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters. The letters usually appear as three white sections through the blur.

Commercial vehicles use yellow licence plates.

Plates in newer coverage can be white too.

NOTE: Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.

Indonesia drives on the left.

NOTE: Malaysia drives on the left, while the Philippines drives on the right.

Indonesia uses white or yellow centre lines. Outer lines will always be white. The centre lines will be solid or dashed.

In Generation 3 coverage, yellow centre lines are more rare, as Indonesia only recently started using this colour for its road lines.

NOTE: Malaysian road lines are always all white.

Poles in Indonesia are typically round and made out of either steel or concrete. Many of the steel poles are painted black, and also feature the Indonesian flag colours on them. The pole tops are usually either even or uneven, depending on the region.

_You can learn more about regional poles in the region-guessing section._

Indonesia commonly uses these black-and-white square or circular bollards, as well as these yellow-and-black ones, which can also have a red reflector. Other designs can also be found.

NOTE: UK-style bollards are mostly found in Kalimantan.

Usually yellow waystones that are angled towards the road, and have a cutout close to the top are unique to Indonesia. They include shorthand for three cities or towns, with the biggest one being on the top in the cutout section.

NOTE: Waystones in the Philippines are perpendicular to the road and have the text facing away from the road.

Indonesian can look very similar to Malaysian, however Indonesian has been influenced by Dutch, and Malaysian by English. These small changes in spelling may help differentiate the two.

An example is the word television in English, which translates to ‘televisi’ in Indonesian, similar to the Dutch word ‘televisie.’ In Malaysian, it translates to ‘televisyen’, more similar to English.
You can find these rows of red and white banners all around Indonesia. Sometimes, more colourful flags can be found.
Cigarette ads can be found all over Indonesia, usually with a black or red colour scheme and around a price of 18,000 Rp. Keep an eye out for illustrated graphic pictures, and the word ‘PERINGATAN’.
Motorcycles in Indonesia have front licence plates, as opposed to other south-east Asian countries which do not.
The official Indonesian currency is the Rupiah (Rp).
Coverage in Indonesia is fairly limited. Notably, there is no coverage on Papua or adjacent islands, and coverage is sparse in areas such as Kalimantan, Aceh, Central Sulawesi and North Maluku.

The names of 2nd level subdivisions, named ‘Kabupaten’ or ‘Kab’ for short, translating to regency, can be found all over Indonesia on various signs and billboards. Each province is split up into multiple Kabupatens, totalling to 417 which are covered by street view, and therefore applicable in Geoguessr. These are learnable with enough time and patience.

_See the resources section for more information._

You can find the cardinal directions written on many addresses. They are as follows:

  • North = Utara
  • East = Timur
  • South = Selatan
  • West = Barat
  • Central = Tengah
  • Southeast = Tenggara

Satellite dishes can help you determine whether you are north or south of the equator. For example, if the satellite dish points north, you are most likely south of it, and vice versa. Additionally, they usually point towards the middle part of West Kalimantan. This lets you use the angle to determine which side of Indonesia you are in. Lastly the angle of the satellite dish can also tell you how far away from the equator you are.

While kabupaten names appear significantly more often, a number of signs also display the postal code. Postal codes are five digits long and grouped by their starting digit, ranging from 1xxxx in Jakarta to 9xxxx in Maluku and Papua.

_You can click on the image to enlarge it._

Indonesia uses two types of pole tops: even and uneven. This refers to the bar that holds the insulators and whether it is symmetrical to the pole itself. Knowing where even and uneven poles are most commonly found is useful for region guessing.
On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra long support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.

You can find these poles with a triangle attachment under the horizontal bar in the following regions.

NOTE: This does not apply to stacked poles.
Poles with an indent on both sides are found in West Java, Jakarta, and Banten.
Trident style pole tops are most commonly found in Central Java and Yogyakarta, and rarely in South and West Kalimantan, and North Sumatra and Riau.
Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.
These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.

Poles with a support shaped like the letter A are common in Kalimantan and the Nusa islands.

NOTE: A-frame poles can exist anywhere where the electrical wires are in a bend and need extra support. Use this tip with caution.

Poles with the flat part of the crossbar facing away from the pole are common in Sulawesi.

NOTE: Usually, poles in Indonesia have the flat part of the crossbar attached to the pole.

You can often see thin, black poles next to regular poles near the East Peninsula of Central Sulawesi. Two pieces of tape can be seen near the top of the poles, usually light blue and green. These can rarely be seen in northern South East Sulawesi.
You can find this rectangle attachment on the pole tops which is mostly unique to Bali. This appears with the Lesser Sunda Island support beam as well.
Pole paint with horizontal text on the pole is usually a good clue for Bali. It is usually dark blue on Bali but can be light blue or even green.
Asymmetrical poles with 2 supports below the bar occur mainly on Sumatra and the southern part of Sulawesi. It is not commonly seen in Kalimantan or Java.
These painted fences are typically found on Sulawesi. They will be mostly painted white with blue or red.
Central Sulawesi features these unique bollards that are painted black on the bottom, white in the middle, and yellow on the top.
Green paint can often be seen on the side of bridges in South and Central Kalimantan.
Within Indonesia, oil palm plantations are mostly concentrated in Sumatra and Kalimantan. Palm plantations can rarely be seen in Sulawesi.

The majority of rice production is concentrated in Java, but can sometimes be found in other provinces, namely South Sulawesi and South Sumatra. They can rarely be found in other provinces as well. For a full overview, see this page.

The Nusas are drier than other regions in Indonesia. Vegetation tends to look less tropical, but instead lower and shrubbier.

NOTE: While less common, other regions such as Java can look similarly dry. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.
Very rounded green hills, typically covered with clusters of palms, sugarcane or corn, are extremely common within the province of Gorontalo.

This savannah landscape is occasionally seen on north Sumba.

NOTE: In Generation 3, you will always see a white car.
Red soil with a layer of white soil on top of it is most commonly found in the Bangka Belitung islands. On these islands, the white soil can often be seen spilling onto the road.

Tiled roofs are most commonly found on the island of Java, and sometimes nearby regions such as southern Sumatra, the Lesser Sunda Islands, and South Kalimantan.

NOTE: The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different. The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.
Plain sheet metal roofs are more commonly found toward the north, where tiled roofs are not found. They are most commonly found on Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra.
Sheet metal roofs with this shape, a symmetrical triangular shape with two levels of sloping, can be found mainly in Sulawesi, but can be found elsewhere in Indonesia.

These horizontal slots inside the triangles of the roofs are almost unique to Southern Sulawesi.

NOTE: They can rarely be found in East Kalimantan and West Nusa.
You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.

Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism. The most important thing to look for are these crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali. Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too. Andesite, a dark, volcanic rock, is a common building material in Bali. You can often see gates, walls, and other intricately carved ornaments built from this material.
West Sumatra features these distinct boat-shaped roofs.

North Sumatra features similarly distinct boat-shaped roofs, however the roofs are less angled upward and they do not feature spires.

NOTE: These roofs are most commonly found near Lake Toba, due to its sacred history.
On Kalimantan, you can find these unique roofs made out of wooden chips.

Roofs with gable horns can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi, Riau and Central and South Kalimantan.

NOTE: Horned roofs are often found with Bugis roofs in South Sulawesi. Use this tip along with other clues to determine which region you are in.

A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs. The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.
Indonesia is religiously a Muslim majority country, so seeing churches, and other Christian signs, is a good clue for these regions.

Generation 3 antenna coverage is most commonly found on Java, but can very rarely be seen on Bali in and around Denpasar. It is most commonly seen in East Java, as most of the antenna coverage in the west has been overwritten by Generation 4.
Black Generation 3 coverage can be found almost everywhere in Indonesia, but is most common in Sulawesi.

This camera glitch, reminiscent of a Moiré Pattern, is found throughout Central Kalimantan.

_You can click on the image for a clearer view._
The region around Lake Toba, in North Sumatra, can be recognized by mountains surrounding the lake and Samosir Island in the middle. Overcast coverage is also common for the region.

Eastern South Kalimantan features these karst formations, particularly along the highway into East Kalimantan.

NOTE: Similar karst formations can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi and West Sumatra.
Palu Bay is a unique slightly north-west facing bay just north of Palu city, which features mountains to the west of the bay, and a flat, more urbanised landscape to the east.
Steeply pitched roofs made of palm tree leaves can sometimes be seen on Nias Island, south west of North Sumatra.
A white SUV with black bars and a wooden plank on the roof can rarely be seen in eastern Bali.
A black cab with men sitting in the truck bed can be seen near Jagasatru on Bali.

steps.html:
GeoGuessr’s own official maps are not very good, for a variety of reasons. Plonk It recommends you play these maps instead:

  • AI Gen - Indonesia (map link) - A well balanced computer generated map of Indonesia with over 100,000 locations.
  • IntersectionGuessr - Indonesia (map link) - Arbitrarily generated locations at intersections, and therefore potentially pinpointable (but this is not guaranteed).

In addition, here are some resources to help you practise Indonesia:

  • Plonk It Indonesia (map link) - This map contains locations for practising each meta in the Plonk It Indonesia guide from step 2 to 3.
  • Kabupaten Practice - Indonesia (map link) - This is a map made for practising kabupatens, containing 5 locations for each and also 3 locations per kota (city).

lm.name: (N) Sumatra Palm (Areca)
lm.note:
Areca palms, often called Sumatra palms w/in indo, basically mostly found within Sumatra. probably most often found in western North Sumatra (and the rest of the west coast). west coast of all of sumatra often hilly, North (eastish) coast often flat.

(i have seen them in the nusas, but you probably shouldnt confuse sumatra w/ the nusas)

lm.name: Bali "thatched" roof
lm.note: bali has these weird thatched lookin roofs, very common in Bali, sometimes in like rice fields, or on side of road etc. does not have to be a full roof for a house

lm.name: Bali Bridge
lm.note: this is what the typical bridge in bali looks like w/ the gold and black. but what makes it unique is the little statue patron things on the ends of the bridge. the actualy stutue thing doesnt have to be there just the pedestal.

lm.name: Bali Hanging things
lm.note: idk what these are, but they are most common on bali.

lm.name: Bali Pavement
lm.note: square bali pavement. not exclusive, but most common.

lm.name: Bali Sticker
lm.note: dark blue sticker on the pole is only found in Bali and Nusa Pineda i think, and i think a lighter version can be found in west nusas maybe lombok aswell, but both can get faded. If you see a blue sticker your prolly somewhere there. most likely bali i think.

lm.name: Bali Walls
lm.note: These two types, the one with this grey bricks, and the orange brick. again not exclusive but quite common on bali.

lm.name: Bangka Belitung roof
lm.note: tiles only on like the creases in the roofs. can be found eslewhere (like nusas i think) but if its on like all the roofs its prolly Bangka Belitung

lm.name: Batam Red Soil
lm.note: Batam has red soil. remember, batam is like an offbrand singapore

lm.name: Batam Vibe
lm.note: if it feels like Singapore, but isnt singapore, its prolly Batam.

lm.name: Bintan constructing
lm.note: bintan is a Batam wannabe. they are basically prepping it to be built up like Batam. So lots of like big buildings with no others around it that seem out of place. Lots of emptiness. click around a little bit and you will get a vibe for it.

lm.name: Cambo Palms
lm.note: idk what exaclty they are called but if you see this palm your prolly in this general area.

lm.name: Central Java Pavement
lm.note: central java pavement. like 80% accurate w/in Java probably.

lm.name: Central Java Pole
lm.note: can be a trident pole but doenst have to be. the way the central insulator is attached to the pole on the side with that extra peice is what makes it unique.

lm.name: Central Kali Camera Glitch
lm.note: I found this camera glitch while searching. If you look 90 degrees to the left of the front of the car, there is a glitch that is easier seen when you zoom in fully with a bunch of little lines. in some panos it is more purple aswell. Found within Central Kali on these roads. some parts may have ben ovverrun with newer coverage. It will have 2024 copyright

lm.name: Central Sula Bollard
lm.note: Central Sulawesi features these unique bollards that are painted black on the bottom, white in the middle, and yellow on the top.

lm.name: East Java Pavement
lm.note: East java pavement. mostly around Surabaya. sometimes called surabaya pavement.

lm.name: East Java Pole
lm.note: uneven pole, which within Java is most likely east java. The unique poles are the ones that are uneven and the pole continues much higher than the crossbar.

lm.name: Flat Lombok
lm.note: Within the Nusas(besides Sumba), if it is flat its prolly Lombok

lm.name: Flat w/ lone mt. w kali
lm.note: west kali is mostly flat, except for the occasional hill or mountain. so you will often see a flat landscape with one or two hills/mountains near you.

lm.name: Flores In the Hills/mountains
lm.note: In the Nusas, and you are in the mountains/tall hills, your probably in Flores

lm.name: Gorontalo Hills
lm.note: Gorontalo has these unique green hills almost roundish rolling hills. sort of a lack of trees, but there are often some oil palms, often corn growing. click around gorontalo and get a vibe for it.

lm.name: Jambi occasional tiled roof
lm.note: jambi has mostly tin roofs w/ the occasional tiled roof. remember gradient from most to least w/in sumatra goes from south to north.

lm.name: Java (and bali) antenna
lm.note: Generation 3 antenna coverage is most commonly found on Java, but can very rarely be seen on Bali in and around Denpasar. It is most commonly seen in East Java, as most of the antenna coverage in the west has been overwritten by Generation 4.

lm.name: Java Rock walls(volcanic)
lm.note: if within Java, and there are these rock walls, (volcanic most likely), and everything feels volcanic, like for ex. dark fields, rocks on the side of the road, etc., you are prolly here.

lm.name: JT road
lm.note: most recognizalbe road in Indonesia. Gen 3, really dry, water north.

lm.name: Kali cut thru forest
lm.note: One way to differentiate Kali from something like Sumatra is that in Kali, most of the roads are like cut through the forest. Everything is bassically on the side of the road again kinda carved into the forest. def more of a vibe

lm.name: Kali uneven poles
lm.note: If you are in Kali, and you have uneven poles, you will NOT be in West Kali

lm.name: Kundur Island soil
lm.note: Kunder island has this orange soil. almost yellowish

lm.name: Lampung Grid
lm.note: Most of Lampung is in a grid, lots of straight rods, not always North-south tho.

lm.name: Lampung Individual houses
lm.note: houses are kinda just all on their own. very spread out. the landscape is flat (in the east, west too difficult). lampung architecture is extremely unique. click around and get a feel for it. the houses almost feel more modern to me, often have collums holding up like a small porch in front. often tiled roofs.

lm.name: Lampung Sticks
lm.note: These sticks on the side of the road are like 100% Lampung 80% of the time. look for other clues cause it could just randomly be like Sulawesi and ur cooked.

lm.name: Lombok roof
lm.note: unique roof. bell shaped.

lm.name: Lombok tiles
lm.note: Lombok often has theses really dark, grey even, tiled roofs.

lm.name: Mahakam River Coal
lm.note: In and around the Mahakam River, you will often see piles of coal being exported.

lm.name: Malay Border roof curve
lm.note: malaysia has this curve on the edges of the roof sometimes. this is not at all of indo origin, so it is only found in places that border malaysia. So mostly on the east coast of Sumatra, all those islands, and West Kalimantan.

lm.name: Mamasa Roof
lm.note: very similar to some of the other roofs, but this one the bottom of the roof that is going up is completely straight and not curved.

lm.name: Mamasa Vibe
lm.note: gen 3 white car, very sunny, can have Mamasa roof, often pines are seen. click around to get a vibe.

lm.name: Medan Other crops
lm.note: within NS around Medan, you often get other crops in addition to Oil palms, like Corn, Sugarcane, etc. (not often rice). Also most of Medan and surrounding local area is in a North-South Grid

lm.name: Muna Island blue houses
lm.note: for some reason Muna Island just has a lot of blue, espcially houses. so if you think u may be in Muna island, and u see blue, its a good clue.

lm.name: Muna Island Vibe
lm.note: lots of blue, kinda dry idk. click around and get a vibe for it you wont miss it.

lm.name: N Maluku layered roofs
lm.note: these layered roofs are quite common in N Maluku

lm.name: N maluku porch roofs
lm.note: like extrusions of roof at a slight down angle are common in North maluku.

lm.name: N Maluku rock
lm.note: North Maluku often has these piles of rock scattered around and then these gutters and other stuff are sometimes made of rock

lm.name: N Maluku rock house foundation
lm.note: houses on North maluku are often on this rock looking foundation that is a bit off the ground.

lm.name: N sula volcanoes
lm.note: north sula has a lot of volcanoes

lm.name: Nias plant
lm.note:
This plant is basically everywhere on the island, and is pretty much unique to Nias island within Indonesia. Recognizable red tinted leaves mixed in with the green leaves.

Being part of North Sumatra, they Nias has the NS poles, often made of metal. Nias also often just has random piles of rock on the side of the road.

lm.name: North Kali blur
lm.note: most of it is overrun. will be front of the car, in northern north kali. also for more car meta: if its gen 3, you probably shoulndt click kali

lm.name: North sula Nice small roads
lm.note: like West sumatra, North sula has these nice small roads

lm.name: North Sumatra Pole
lm.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.

lm.name: Northern Sula Pole
lm.note: Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.

lm.name: NS lake landscape
lm.note: Hills are cleared of trees, very green (if there are trees they are replanted, standing on their own, not natural looking). mostly a vibe but nothing else in indo looks like this. Hills with nothing on it exept grass = lake

lm.name: NS lake roof
lm.note:
Around the Lake in North Sumatra you get this roof (central NS). Very boat shaped. can often be found as miniature roofs like on side of the road or on shacks or on top of stuff, etc.

DO NOT confuse it with the West Sumatra roof, that one the ends are steeper and go higher and are "spiky".

lm.name: NS mount sinabung
lm.note: Very distinct Volcano visible from a decently far away around Berastagi. Also in the plateau the crops are different, farming equipment is differnt, often greenhouses, very small fields. overall very different culture from rest of NS.

lm.name: NS ugly building
lm.note: block building with no nice things on the side (just concrete). Often above a garage (even if a building is one story, it can often still have a blocky or square feel which is a good clue for NS). Often found in rows, all next to each other This is a good clue for North Sumatra and Sometimes Riau.

lm.name: Nusa Banana Plant
lm.note: If within the Nusas, u think u might be in Flores, and see banana plants, its prolly east.

lm.name: Nusa Penida
lm.note: Like Bali, has basically everything bali has, but a bit more dry, has a vibe to the landscape. click around to get a feel for it.

lm.name: Nusa Pole
lm.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present. The Nusas are very dry.

lm.name: Palu NSish Ridges
lm.note: The city of Palu in in a roughly north south valley with large mountains on either side.

lm.name: Pipes to Dumai
lm.note: lots of oil palms in riau. Dumai is the main port so the palm oil is exported through pipes to Dumai. If you see pipes, you think you might be in Riau, your probably around Dumai.

lm.name: Pontianak Canals
lm.note: Pontianak has a lot of Canals and waterways running through it. good clue for the west coast of Kali overall.

lm.name: Rante Poa Roof
lm.note: A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs. The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.

lm.name: Riau Oil Palms
lm.note: Oil Palms = click Riau basically. Riau has a lot of oil palms.

lm.name: Riau pole marking
lm.note: within Riau, an oval that says "KJ" in it, w/ blue writing around the oval.

lm.name: Riau Roof thing
lm.note: This specific Gable Horn (i think thats what its called) is unique to Riau.

lm.name: S Kali pole sticker
lm.note: silver reflective thing wrapped around the pole, found in S Kali and the majors roads that lead out of it.

lm.name: S/C Kali green bridge
lm.note: Green paint can often be seen on the side of bridges in South and Central Kalimantan.

lm.name: SE Sula grid
lm.note: southeast sula is often in a grid like lampung, can look like lampung at times

lm.name: South Sula Roof
lm.note: this shape of roof with the trinagle and then the flaps coming off the sides at a different angle is extremely common in South Sula. They also often have gable horns. The more unique ones have peices of wood horizontal supporting the top triangle

lm.name: South Sumatra Architecture
lm.note: often tiled roofs, with wooden front of the house. House is kinda elevated off the ground. once you see it you wont unsee it.

lm.name: South Sumatra Rubber Trees
lm.note: Lots of rubber trees in South sumatra. Ive also seen them in north sumatra though, but should be able to tell the difference w/ other clues w/in Sumatra

lm.name: SS mixed side plantations
lm.note: South Sumatra has terrible land management. so if you feel like the land is being poorly managed, its prolly south sumatra. one effect of this is that there are often mixed types of plantations on each side of the road, or a plantation on one side, and then its wild on the other, etc.

lm.name: Stereotypical Bali Roofs
lm.note: Tiled roofs, often have a crown, and the things on the corners of the roof also.

lm.name: Sula Fence
lm.note: These painted fences are typically found on Sulawesi. They will be mostly painted white with blue or red.

lm.name: Sumatra (southern)  bright tiles
lm.note: very bright tiles tiles mixed in with the "normal" colored tiles. you wont really see this in java. remember theres a gradient of how many roofs are tiled from Lampung to Jambi.

lm.name: Sumba Hills
lm.note: If in the Nusas, and are in the hills (not mountains/taller hills like Flores) you are probably in Sumbra, mostly west/south

lm.name: Sumba Roof
lm.note: You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.

lm.name: Sumba Savannah
lm.note:
Sumba is the only place that has this extremely flat, extremely dry Savannah landscape.

if gen 3, it will be white car

lm.name: Sumbawa Fence
lm.note: Within the Nusas, the Sulawesi style fence is common on the Island of Sumbawa.

lm.name: Sumbawa inbetween hills
lm.note: most of the coverage in Sumbawa is in between the hills/mountains in the flat areas. So if you are in the Nusas, but in flat area between mountains/hills (you can see them in the distance) you are prolly in Sumbawa.

lm.name: Timor Roofs
lm.note: these "thatched" roofs are exclusive to Timor. Usually southeast.

lm.name: Timor white brick
lm.note: If you think u might be on Timor, (very dry, has a distinct vibe cause its the most east), white brick buildings are a good clue for Timor.

NOTE: This does not apply to stacked poles

lm.name: W Kali red dirt

lm.name: W Kali/Maluku pole

lm.name: Indonesia
lm.note:
Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters. The letters usually appear as three white sections through the blur.

Commercial vehicles use yellow licence plates.

Plates in newer coverage can be white too.

NOTE: Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.

lm.name: Agriculture - Cassava
lm.note: Cassava (Manihot esculenta) can be recognised by its small, hand-shaped leaves. It can be found both in plantations as well as semi-wild in residential areas. It is most commonly seen in Lampung and Java with Lampung being the main hot spot.

lm.name: Agriculture - Oil Palms
lm.note: Within Indonesia, oil palm plantations are mostly concentrated in Sumatra and Kalimantan. Palm plantations can rarely be seen in Sulawesi.

lm.name: Agriculture - Rice
lm.note: The majority of rice production is concentrated in Java, but can sometimes be found in other provinces, namely South Sulawesi and South Sumatra. They can rarely be found in other provinces as well.

lm.name: Architecture - Andesite
lm.note: Andesite, a dark, volcanic rock, is a common building material in Bali. You can often see gates, walls, and other intricately carved ornaments built from this material.

lm.name: Architecture - Bali Architecture
lm.note: Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism. The most important thing to look for are these crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali. Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too.

lm.name: Architecture - Boat Roof - Not Spiky
lm.note:
North Sumatra features similarly distinct boat-shaped roofs, however the roofs are less angled upward and they do not feature spires.

NOTE: These roofs are most commonly found near Lake Toba, due to its sacred history.

lm.name: Architecture - Boat Roof - Spiky
lm.note: West Sumatra features these distinct boat-shaped roofs.

lm.name: Architecture - Flat Tiles
lm.note: The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different. The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.

lm.name: Architecture - Horny Roof
lm.note:
Roofs with gable horns can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi, Riau and Central and South Kalimantan.

NOTE: Horned roofs are often found with Bugis roofs in South Sulawesi. Use this tip along with other clues to determine which region you are in.

lm.name: Architecture - Java Roof
lm.note:
Tiled roofs are most commonly found on the island of Java, and sometimes nearby regions such as southern Sumatra, the Lesser Sunda Islands, and South Kalimantan.

NOTE: The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different. The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.

lm.name: Architecture - Malay Canopies
lm.note: In the regions of Sumatra and Kalimantan that lie opposite Malaysia, many buildings have metal canopies with curved ends. These canopies are often blue or red.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Roof
lm.note: Steeply pitched roofs made of palm tree leaves can sometimes be seen on Nias Island, south west of North Sumatra.

lm.name: Architecture - Sheet Roofs
lm.note: Plain sheet metal roofs are more commonly found toward the north, where tiled roofs are not found. They are most commonly found on Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra.

lm.name: Architecture - South Sula House
lm.note:
These horizontal slots inside the triangles of the roofs are almost unique to Southern Sulawesi.

NOTE: They can rarely be found in East Kalimantan and West Nusa.

lm.name: Architecture - Sumba Roof
lm.note: You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.

lm.name: Architecture - Tongkonan
lm.note: A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs. The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.

lm.name: Architecture - Wooden Chips Roof
lm.note: On Kalimantan, you can find these unique roofs made out of wooden chips.

lm.name: Car Meta - Gen 3 Antenna
lm.note: Generation 3 antenna coverage is most commonly found on Java, but can very rarely be seen on Bali in and around Denpasar. It is most commonly seen in East Java, as most of the antenna coverage in the west has been overwritten by Generation 4.

lm.name: Car Meta - Gen 3 Black
lm.note: Black Generation 3 coverage can be found almost everywhere in Indonesia, but is most common in Sulawesi.

lm.name: Car Meta - Jagasatru Car
lm.note: A black cab with men sitting in the truck bed can be seen near Jagasatru on Bali.

lm.name: Car Meta - Wooden Plank Car
lm.note: A white SUV with black bars and a wooden plank on the roof can rarely be seen in eastern Bali.

lm.name: Coverage Meta - Pink Air
lm.note: In some of the Generation 4 coverage in the city of Batam, a purple tint and a black blurred object can be seen. Although this camera glitch is most commonly found in Batam, you may spot it in nearby regions such as North Sumatra, around Medan. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Cigarette Blocks
lm.note: Central Sulawesi features these unique bollards that are painted black on the bottom, white in the middle, and yellow on the top.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Even Pole
lm.note: Indonesia uses two types of pole tops: even and uneven. This refers to the bar that holds the insulators and whether it is symmetrical to the pole itself. Knowing where even and uneven poles are most commonly found is useful for region guessing.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Green Bridge
lm.note: Green paint can often be seen on the side of bridges in South and Central Kalimantan.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Indented Pole
lm.note: Poles with an indent on both sides are found in West Java, Jakarta, and Banten.

lm.name: Infrastructure - North Sumatra Pole
lm.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Nusa Pole
lm.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands ('Nusas'), you can find poles with an extra long support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Pole Tape
lm.note: You can often see thin, black poles next to regular poles near the East Peninsula of Central Sulawesi. Two pieces of tape can be seen near the top of the poles, usually light blue and green. These can rarely be seen in northern South East Sulawesi.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Rectangle Attachment
lm.note: Bali features both even and uneven poles, as well as the Lesser Sunda island variants. You can also find this unique rectangle attachment on the pole tops in Bali.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Sulawesi Fences
lm.note: These painted fences are typically found on Sulawesi. They will be mostly painted white with blue or red.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Surabaya Pavement
lm.note: Pavement made out of bricks like this is found in East Java, particularly around Surabaya

lm.name: Infrastructure - Trapezoid Pole
lm.note: Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Triangle Attachment
lm.note:
You can find these poles with a triangle attachment under the horizontal bar in the following regions.

NOTE: This does not apply to stacked poles.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Trident Pole
lm.note: Trident style pole tops are most commonly found in Central Java and Yogyakarta, and rarely in South and West Kalimantan, and North Sumatra and Riau.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Uneven Pole
lm.note: Indonesia uses two types of pole tops: even and uneven. This refers to the bar that holds the insulators and whether it is symmetrical to the pole itself. Knowing where even and uneven poles are most commonly found is useful for region guessing.

lm.name: Landscape - Dryness
lm.note:
The Nusas typically look drier than other regions in Indonesia. The islands get especially dry towards the east, especially in Generation 3. Vegetation tends to look less tropical, but instead more brown with a lack of leaves. Sumba Island is also the driest of the Nusas.

NOTE: While less common, other regions such as Java can look similarly dry. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Landscape - Lake Toba
lm.note: The region around Lake Toba, in North Sumatra, can be recognized by mountains surrounding the lake and Samosir Island in the middle. Overcast coverage is also common for the region.

lm.name: Landscape - Palu Bay
lm.note: Palu Bay is a unique slightly north-west facing bay just north of Palu city, which features mountains to the west of the bay, and a flat, more urbanised landscape to the east.

lm.name: Landscape - Red Soil
lm.note: Red soil can often be found on Batam and the Bangka Belitung islands, located east of mainland Sumatra.

lm.name: Landscape - Savannah
lm.note:
This savannah landscape is occasionally seen on North Sumba.

NOTE: In Generation 3, you will always see a white car.

lm.name: Misc - Christianity
lm.note: Indonesia is religiously a Muslim majority country, so seeing churches, and other Christian signs, is a good clue for these regions.

lm.name: Vegetation - Areca
lm.note: Areca palms (Areca catechu) are most prominent in western Sumatra; however they can also be seen elsewhere less commonly. They can be recognised by their relatively short and thick leaves.

lm.name: Vegetation - Coastal She-Oak
lm.note: Coastal she-oak (Casuarina equisetifolia) can be found along the coast throughout much of the country, but particularly in Sumatra, Kalimantan and Java. Their leaves resemble the needles of pine trees, but are noticeably longer. Another species of she-oak can be found in mountainous regions throughout the country.

lm.name: Vegetation - Coconut
lm.note: Coconut palms (Cocos nucifera) can be found in many regions throughout Indonesia, but are most abundant along the coast, especially in western Sumatra, southern Java, northern Sulawesi and North Maluku.

lm.name: Vegetation - Footstool Palm
lm.note: Footstool palm (Saribus rotundifolius) has fan-shaped leaves similar to those of Palmyra palm; however the crown is more open, the leaves are thinner and the palm itself is usually taller. It can be found most notably in Sulawesi and more rarely in other parts of the country.

lm.name: Vegetation - Gebang Palm
lm.note: Gebang palm (Corypha utan) can at first glance look similar to both Palmyra and footstool palm due to its fan-shaped leaves, however the leaves are noticeably larger, stiffer and more upright in contrast to the round crown shape of both Palmyra and footstool palm. Unlike most palms, the gebang palm will only flower once at the end of its life in a dramatic gesture where the leaves wither away and it shoots one large inflorescence into the heavens before it dies. It is found mainly in the east of the country, namely Sulawesi and the Nusas.

lm.name: Vegetation - Milkweed
lm.note: Giant milkweed (Calotropis gigantea) is a small shrub with thick round leaves and pale flowers. It can be found in dry regions of Indonesia, namely the Nusas and parts of Java and Sulawesi.

lm.name: Vegetation - Palmyra
lm.note: Palmyra palms (Borassus flabellifer) can be recognised by their fan-shaped leaves and dense round crowns. Compared to footstool palm, the crown is more dense, the leaves are heavier and the palm itself is usually shorter. It is found in dry parts of the country, namely the Nusas and South Sulawesi.

lm.name: Vegetation - Sumatran Pine
lm.note: Sumatran pines (Pinus merkusii) in Indonesia can be found in a few pockets across the country, notable areas include North Sumatra and Java. They can be recognised by having long needles for leaves, but be careful not to confuse them with she-oak, which has even longer leaves.

lm.name: Vegetation - White Leadtree
lm.note: White leadtree (Leucaena leucocephala) can be recognised by its delicate featherlike (bipinnate) leaves. Fruits are often also visible in the form of legume pods. It can be found mainly in the Nusas as well as a few other dry areas of the country.

lm.name: Arrow Roof Extensions
lm.note: Roofs featuring an arrow-shaped extension protruding upwards are common in the eastern half of Java.

lm.name: Baroque Ornate Rooftops
lm.note:
Various styles of thick, baroque-style ornately-decorated rooftops can be found in East Java.

Ornate rooftops featuring these semicircular openings, usually disconnected at the bottom, can be found in western East Java.

Ornate rooftops featuring these tripoint designs are further localised within western East Java. They often, but not always, also feature the semicircular openings noted above.

lm.name: Bawean Island Dhurung Bawean
lm.note: Dhurung Bawean is a traditional architectural structure on the Indonesian island of Bawean, which serves as a lumbung (storehouse) for harvests and as an outdoor gathering place for social activities and guests. It is characterised by an unusually large roof structure supported by wooden pillars.

lm.name: Bawean Island Red Ridge Tiles
lm.note: Roofs similar to those found on Bangka Island are very common. These typically consist of fibre cement sheets and** reddish tiles lining the edges**. The second type of roof that is also frequently found is the fully tiled Javanese roof.

lm.name: Brick Ornaments
lm.note: In a similar area, you will find roof ridges spanned by perforated bricks.

lm.name: Candi Bentar
lm.note: Candi Bentar or “split gates” appear like a single structure split into two and are vestiges of Hinduism on Java. The sides facing each other are plain while the outsides may be highly ornate. They may be red brick or painted. They can be found at historic sites across Java but are most common in East Java.

lm.name: Curled Metal Sheets
lm.note: Thin metal sheets with curled ends spanning the roof ridges are a common sight across most of eastern Central Java. They also frequently feature a central ornament displaying the year of construction.

lm.name: Double-Pitched-Roofs
lm.note: The simplest of the three roof types is the Double-Pitched-Roof. It is characterised by a multi-angled roof structure, but with only two different roof angles. Each roof surface is parallel to the long side of the house.

lm.name: Downward Pointing Finials
lm.note: Many Javanese roofs feature narrow, vertical wooden attachments at or below the end of the roof ridge. They often appear as an upward or downward pointed arrow, but can feature a wide range of designs (e.g., heart, anchor, fork). Regardless of shape, these attachments are found commonly in East Java and also appear routinely in Central Java and Yogyakarta. Note that similar designs can sometimes be found outside Java.

lm.name: Flexible Roof Sheets
lm.note: Flexible roof sheets are very common around Pulosari and Watoekoempoel in western Central Java, as well as in the villages south of Mount Lawu in the far eastern part of the province.

lm.name: Hindu Shrines
lm.note:
The area around Mount Bromo, especially along its northern face surrounding Wonokitri, is home to the Tenggerese - the last Hindu-majority people in Java.

The region features many Hindu design elements, the most distinct being these small shrines (Pelinggih) which are often found at intersections or in front of homes.

The region can be differentiated from Bali by the very mountainous setting with lots of mountain casuarina (she-oak) trees.

lm.name: Jakarta Industrial Parks
lm.note: A lot of industrial parks can be found near the outskirts of Jakarta Metropolitan Area.

lm.name: Jakarta Narrow Alleys
lm.note: Jakarta has many narrow alleys where pedestrians, motorcycles and cars travel. Sometimes you can see skyscrapers in the distance.

lm.name: Jepara Kudus Pati Ornaments
lm.note: Small tooth-like embellishments and filigree motifs along the ridge and edges of the roof are common in the regencies of Jepara, Kudus and Pati. Rare examples also exist further south.

lm.name: Joglo
lm.note: Joglo houses feature a steep ‘hat’ shaped roof surrounded by large flaps on all four sides.

lm.name: Joglo Bocokan
lm.note: Rembang Regency is home to a unique traditional house known as the Joglo Bocokan. It is characterised by a Joglo base with gables on the sides, as opposed to slopes. A small transverse roof may or may not be present inside the gable.

lm.name: Lavu Ornaments
lm.note: South-west of Mount Lawu, located in eastern Central Java, metal triangles with jagged edges can be seen adorning the end of roof ridges on corrugated metal rooftops.

lm.name: Leuit
lm.note: In the southeastern mountainous part of Banten, traditional Sundanese rice barns known as Leuit are still common.

lm.name: Limasan
lm.note: Limasan roofs also have a multi-angled roof structure, but unlike Joglo roofs, they are shallower and the flap is only present on two sides.

lm.name: Limestone Bricks Grey Mortar
lm.note: Limestone bricks are common in northern East Java, including Madura Island, reflecting the limestone geology of the area. The bricks are put together with thick grey mortar, creating a striking visual distinction.

lm.name: Madura Cement Ridges
lm.note: **Roof ridges made out of smooth cement **are quite common on Madura, especially on Limasan-style roofs. Some roofs on Madura feature these stubby concrete spikes on each end of the rooftop.

lm.name: Madura Limestone Bricks Red Mortar
lm.note: In the eastern part of Madura Island, houses feature walls made of white bricks and thick red mortar instead of grey, reflecting the local geology.

lm.name: Madura Small Stilt Houses
lm.note: Small stilt houses with Limasan roofs are often found near traditional Madurese settlements. These stilts sometimes rest on stone foundations.

lm.name: Madura Traditional Settlements
lm.note: Traditional Madurese settlements, called Tanèyan Lanjhang, consist of two or more buildings arranged around a rectangular courtyard. The main building often joins two or more identical units together.

lm.name: Metal Eaves
lm.note: Metal eaves installed along the edges of the roof are highly localised to the northeastern part of Central Java. Metal eaves most commonly come in the colours blue, green, or red.

lm.name: Metal Roofs
lm.note: Although Java is well-known for its tiled roofs, communities featuring heavy or predominant use of metal roofs can be found in a number of mountainous and coastal areas on Java. Notable examples include the areas surrounding Mount Slamet (Central Java) and Mount Bromo (East Java).

lm.name: Neat Hedges
lm.note: Villages located along the southern coastal plain of Central Java, particularly in the regions stretching west of Yogyakarta, are characterised by an organised layout of small rectangular properties framed by short, neatly-trimmed hedges. These settlements mostly follow a strict grid-like pattern with a noticeable absence of winding roads.

lm.name: Ornamental Gate Pillars
lm.note: Roads flanked by these standalone decorative entrance pillars are common in East Java, eastern Central Java, and Yogyakarta. These may mark the entrance to a property or village.

lm.name: Pati Rembang Ornaments
lm.note: Highly decorated metal or concrete triangles are seen spanning the entire ridges of roofs in Pati and Rembang regencies.

lm.name: Ridge Ends Octogonal
lm.note: Conversely, roof ridge ends with a roughly octagonal shape are common in East Java, but are very rare on the rest of the island. Note that the diagonal sides are usually curved inward, somewhat resembling a plus (“+”) shape.

lm.name: Ridge Ends Pentagonal
lm.note: The ends of roof ridges in Java have various shapes that can be helpful for narrowing down your location on the island. Roof ridge ends in a pentagonal shape are common in Banten, West Java and Central Java, but are quite rare in East Java.

lm.name: Ridge Ends Potruding
lm.note: In East Java, ridge ends often stick out a small distance past the end of the roof itself. This can be very subtle, but in the right lighting it can sometimes be identified by the presence of a small shadow underneath the ridge end.

lm.name: Roof Ornaments
lm.note: Diverse roof ornaments are a common sight throughout East Java as well as eastern Central Java. These roof ornaments mostly feature winged or curled shapes and animal motifs, located at the ends and peaks of roof ridges.

lm.name: Stacked Tiles
lm.note: Ridges featuring multiple stacked roof tiles are particularly common in the eastern part of Central Java. You will also spot this feature in some areas of East Java.

lm.name: Staggered Tiles
lm.note: Roof tiles with this staggered, alternating pattern can be found throughout Java, but are most common in East Java and adjacent parts of Central Java.

lm.name: Stone Pedestal Houses
lm.note: Throughout Banten and the mountainous south of West Java, many houses rest on stone pedestals, leaving the natural ground beneath exposed. These stone bases provide a level foundation, compensating for the uneven terrain in rural areas.

lm.name: Thatched Roofs
lm.note: Thatched roofs are a common sight throughout Banten, especially in rural regions. While they aren't unique to Banten and appear sporadically in other parts of Java, high concentrations are found only here and in a small section of West Java.

lm.name: Winged Ornaments
lm.note: These distinctive Balinese-style roof ornaments, consisting of long flat wing shapes with curled ends can be found in the far eastern end of Java.

lm.name: Zi8gzag Wings
lm.note: Around Mount Merbabu (just north of Yogyakarta) the Mount Merbabu zi8gzag wings occur. Small, wing-like structures, almost always in a zigzag pattern, adorn the ends of roof ridges.

lm.name: Banjar Chief Houses (Bubungan Tinggi)
lm.note: In parts of South Kalimantan, you can see the traditional chieftains’ houses of the Banjar people. These are known as Rumah Bubungan Tinggi, meaning 'high peak' houses, due to their steep gable roofs. The whole house is built on top of high stilts.

lm.name: Bright Yellow
lm.note: In the coastal cities of West Kalimantan, especially Pontianak, you will occasionally see bright-yellow buildings and monuments. The colour dates back to the Pontianak Sultanate, where yellow signified Malay royalty, and the tradition has persisted locally.

lm.name: Buginese Features
lm.note: Simple, elevated houses built on wooden stilts with Buginese roof features can be found along the north-east coast of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Chinese Architecture
lm.note: Along the west coast of West Kalimantan, especially in the northwest and the city of Singkawang, you will notice a lot of Chinese architecture and inscriptions. As well as the distinctive paifang-style gates and klenteng (temples), there are many Chinese cemeteries with characteristic rounded, horseshoe-shaped tombs. Similar features appear across Indonesia wherever there are sizable Chinese communities, but West Kalimantan has the largest Chinese population in Indonesia.

lm.name: Colorful Houses
lm.note: The further north-east you go in Kalimantan, the more likely you are to find houses painted in bright colours.

lm.name: Dayak Features
lm.note:
The Dayak are the indigenous people of Borneo and generally inhabit more inland parts of the island. Malinau, Kutai Barat and Sintang regencies have the most prominent Dayak populations.

Dayak traditional art is extremely intricate and curvy and can be found painted on walls, fences, poles and other surfaces. Key motifs include the Aso (a mythical hybrid of a dog and dragon representing strength), the Hornbill (symbolising nobility and bravery), and an elongated hexagonal shield.

lm.name: Gable Rosette Designs
lm.note: Rosette designs on gables are fairly common in West Kalimantan. They can be seen elsewhere in Indonesia too, but within Kalimantan, they are most likely to be seen in West Kalimantan.

lm.name: Hindu Structures
lm.note: In the south of South Kalimantan you will find many of the same features that are associated with Lampung, including Hindu religious structures, property entrance wing walls, and sticks used as bollards.

lm.name: Horizontal Boards
lm.note: Banjarese houses in South Kalimantan have wide, horizontal boards spanning the top of the front of the houses. These boards can be wooden or metal.

lm.name: Jerkinhead Roofs
lm.note: Many modern houses in South Kalimantan incorporate elements of the traditional Banjarese traditional Gajah Manusu houses. In particular, they often feature its signature jerkinhead roof.

lm.name: Lampung Style Roofs
lm.note: Within Kalimantan, Lampung-style tiled roofs are found in the provinces of Central, South and East Kalimantan.

lm.name: Long Wooden Walkways
lm.note: Houses with long wooden walkways leading up to them from the road are more common towards North and East Kalimantan, but are found sporadically across all of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Malay Style Halls
lm.note: Monumental Malay-style halls appear occasionally in West Kalimantan. Typical features include a broad central staircase, spacious verandas and numerous tall stilts. You will also find modern variants that keep only some elements, principally the grand, columned look.

lm.name: Traditional Longhouses
lm.note: The traditional longhouse is the most iconic architectural form of the Dayak people across Kalimantan and is the core of their communal and social life. These longhouses are more common inland and in northern parts of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Vertical Panel Doors
lm.note: Houses in the south-east of Kalimantan sometimes feature a prominent set of uniform vertical panels that serve as the main front access to the house. The panels are framed in a distinct colour creating a striking facade.

lm.name: Wooden Shingles
lm.note: Houses with traditional wooden shingles are present in Central, South and East Kalimantan.

lm.name: Wooden Swiftlet Towers
lm.note: These tall wooden towers are used for farming swallows’ nests, a Chinese delicacy. Concrete versions of the structure are common across Kalimantan; however, the wooden variant is mostly only present in the eastern half of Kalimantan.

lm.name: North Maluku - Modern Sasadu Houses
lm.note: At the northern tip of North Maluku, modern versions of the traditional Sasadu house with a highly recognisable metal roof construction can be found. The roof shape consists of a Bangla roof with a particularly protruding gable.

lm.name: Alor Arrow-Tip Shaped Roofs
lm.note: Traditional houses on Alor have a characteristic arrow-tip shape, are raised on stilts and feature thatched or sheet metal roofs.

lm.name: Alor Brick Bamboo Houses
lm.note: Houses on Alor often have a lower section made of brick and an upper section made of woven bamboo matting.

lm.name: Alor Elongated Stone Walls
lm.note: Long rock walls are common on Alor. However unlike those on Rote, these walls are not made from limestone, so the stones are smoother, like large pebbles.

lm.name: Alor Mesh Window Coverings
lm.note: Windows with bamboo mesh coverings are also a distinctive feature of houses on Alor.

lm.name: Alor, Lembata & Adonara Wide Spaced Fences
lm.note: Bamboo fences on Alor, Lembata and Adonara have noticeably large open spaces between both horizontal and vertical bamboo bars.

lm.name: Bali Candi Bentar
lm.note: These beautifully carved split gates, known as Candi Bentar, are a quintessential element of Balinese Hindu architecture. On Bali, they are predominantly crafted from dark, volcanic basalt. While they typically mark property entrances, they occasionally appear on public roads as well.

lm.name: Bali Dragon Tail (Penjor)
lm.note: A Penjor is an elaborately decorated, long bamboo pole that serves as an important ritual object in Balinese Hinduism.

lm.name: Bali High Stone Walls
lm.note: In Bali, properties are typically enclosed by high stone walls, often adorned with basalt ornamentation.

lm.name: Bali Roof Ornaments
lm.note: Roof ornaments are a staple of Balinese architecture. Common features include crown-like decorations and wing-like finials at the roof ridge ends, often combined with a central element. These designs are also present in western Lombok and in neighbouring East Java, which have large Balinese populations

lm.name: Flores Conical Houses
lm.note: Western Flores is inhabited by the Manggarai people and their villages are usually centred around a traditional chieftain's house with a conical roof and a distinctive finial.

lm.name: Flores Hat Roofs
lm.note: Roofs shaped like hats are common in central Flores in areas that are ethnically Ngada, Nage and Ende. There is a very high concentration in the ethnically Ngada area around Bajawa where the houses also have distinct ornaments on both ends of the top beam.

lm.name: Komodo Buginese Houses
lm.note: Inhabitants of Komodo Island are descendants of Bugis from Sulawesi and of former convicts who were abandoned on the island. Buginese architecture therefore dominates, with triangular gables and gable horns. Green and blue are the most common colours, and houses are often built on stilts. Property boundaries are sometimes marked with loose rocks.

lm.name: Lombok Curved Roofs
lm.note: This curved roof shape in Lombok is influenced by the traditional rice barns of the Sasak tribe. Whilst rice barns in their traditional form are rare, their influence can be seen in the shapes of houses, gates and shelters throughout Lombok.

lm.name: Lombok Tiles & Walls
lm.note: Apart from ordinary Javanese tiles, roofs made of grey tiles are almost exclusive to Lombok. Another feature of Lombok architecture is the grey concrete block walls that surround properties.

lm.name: Red Bricks
lm.note: Red brick houses are widespread on the Nusa islands of Sumbawa and Alor. They also occur on Lombok, Flores, Lembata and Adonara, but less frequently.

lm.name: Rote Palm Stalk Fences
lm.note: Fences made from palm stalks in a tight wicker-weave pattern are common on Rote.

lm.name: Rote Piled-Up Stone Walls
lm.note: On Rote, plots of land and fields are surrounded by distinctive long walls made from piled-up stones.

lm.name: Sumba Bamboo Houses
lm.note: Houses made entirely of bamboo materials with sheet metal roofs are also frequently found on Sumba.

lm.name: Sumba Graves
lm.note: Graves on the predominantly Christian Sumba are often in the shape of a rectangular frustum with a flat table-like top.

lm.name: Sumba High Pitched Roofs
lm.note: The traditional houses of Sumba, known as Uma Mbatangu, feature soaring, high-pitched roofs that taper dramatically into a pointed apex, which is decorated on both sides with upright finials.

lm.name: Sumba Western Thatched Roofs
lm.note: On the western tip of Sumba you can find these types of traditional houses with thatched roofs. The white brick houses typical of the Nusas are also found all over Sumba.

lm.name: Sumbawa Buginese Tiled Roofs
lm.note: A good indicator for Sumbawa is tiled Buginese houses. These are recognisable by their tiled horizontal roof flap across the gable. The tiles are often the same style that is found on Java. This style of tile is not found on Sulawesi. These houses also typically lack balconies and are surrounded by fences.

lm.name: Sumbawa Metall Fences
lm.note: On Sumbawa, you will find an unusually high number of sheet metal fences compared to the rest of Indonesia. Fences and gates made of bamboo are also common.

lm.name: Sumbawa Tiled And Metall Roofs
lm.note: Sumbawa marks the boundary of the transition from tiled roofs to sheet metal roofs. While a mix of both can be found on the island’s west side, the east side is dominated by sheet metal roofing.

lm.name: Timor & Rote Timber Frame Houses
lm.note: The most distinctive house types on Timor feature a boxy timber frame central section infilled with palm or bamboo. This type of house may also rarely be found on Rote.

lm.name: Timor Spherical Shape Houses
lm.note: Traditional bamboo houses with thatched roofs are found scattered across Timor. These houses sometimes have a circular shape. Modern versions with metal roofs can also be found. Unlike Manggarai chieftain houses, these often have a short ridge with two small horns along the top.

lm.name: Westnusa Pavilions
lm.note: These pavilions on stilts with a pyramidal roof can be found throughout Lombok and Sumbawa.

lm.name: White Bricks
lm.note: White brick houses are widespread on the Nusa islands of Timor, Rote and Sumba while red brick houses are much less common.

lm.name: Selayar Island - Buginese Architecture
lm.note:
The architecture of Selayar Island is characterised by the large number of Bugis-style houses. These sometimes have thatched gables. Modern houses typically have fibre cement roofs with sheet metal lining the edges.

Note: The elements mentioned are to be understood as a combination specific to Selayar Island. Individual elements, such as fiber cement roofs with metal lining, also occur elsewhere.

lm.name: Bamboo Fences
lm.note: In addition to Sula fences, many bamboo fences can be found in the southern part of the South East Sulawesi.

lm.name: Bamboo-Lattice Pavilions
lm.note: In the southern part of South Sulawesi, including Selayar Island, you can sometimes find bamboo-lattice pavilions. These mark the entryway from the roadside to a household property and range from simple flat arches to small roofed pavilions.

lm.name: Brick Manufacturing
lm.note: Brick manufacturing is common across Peleng Island. White bricks and sometimes the sand needed for their production, can be seen stored along the narrow roads.

lm.name: Buginese Architecture
lm.note:
Bugis houses are typically elongated wooden stilt houses elevated well above the ground.

They are topped by a simple gabled roof. The front gable often features a distinctive finial. The houses also have a gable end formed from panels and with a distinctive shape. The number of overlapping panels indicates the social status of the owner.

Access to these houses is via a steep, usually single-flight staircase leading directly to a protruding open or semi-open veranda.

lm.name: Bulge Roofs
lm.note:
As well as the traditional Tongkonan houses with saddle-shaped roofs, the area around Tana Toraja contains houses influenced by both the local traditional architecture and Buginese architecture. These commonly feature multi-layered gable roofs with a slight bulge at the end.

This roof type can also be found in two other areas: one south of Lake Matano and another east of Lake Poso in Central Sulawesi.

lm.name: Buol Green Yellow
lm.note: Meanwhile, Buol Regency favours a green and yellow colour scheme. You will see these colours on political posters, official buildings, fences, and monuments. However, keep in mind that the majority of Sula fences here remain mostly blue and white, similar to those in Toli-Toli Regency.

lm.name: Central Grey Bricks
lm.note: Architecture in Central Sulawesi is defined by its simplicity. Throughout the province, simple wooden houses are very common, but the most widespread building material is unplastered grey brick, which is far more prevalent than red brick. It is common to see houses where the front facade has been painted while the sides remain exposed and unplastered.

lm.name: Central Sulawesi Hedges
lm.note: Throughout Central Sulawesi, villages are characterised by neatly maintained, low-growing hedges that frequently feature blooming pink flowers.

lm.name: Dondo Houses
lm.note: Toli-Toli Regency is the home of the Dondo people. Their traditional dwellings are very simple, rustic-looking wooden houses built on stilts. These structures are typically longer than they are wide and are built from raw, untreated wood. They also feature gable roofs and simple wooden bridges leading to the entrance.

lm.name: Dutch Colonial Architecture
lm.note: The old town area around the harbour of** Donggala** featured well-preserved Dutch colonial architecture. Most striking are the buildings with** rounded corners,** a design element rarely seen elsewhere in Indonesia.

lm.name: Grid Layouts & Hedges
lm.note: Many villages in South East Sulawesi have grid-like layouts and well-maintained hedges, which are often strikingly long.

lm.name: Hindu Architecture South-East
lm.note: In the central southern part of South East Sulawesi, you can find a lot of Hindu-related architecture.

lm.name: Hindu Gardens Central
lm.note: Cultural influences are also visible in the landscape; small Hindu gardens featuring statues are present throughout the province, with particular hotspots located on the Banggai Peninsula and along the coast south of Parigi.

lm.name: Mamasa Roofs
lm.note: Banua, the traditional houses of the Mamasa people in West Sulawesi, have distinctive roofs. These are arched with curves upwards at both ends. They are usually asymmetrical, with one of the ends taller than the other. Ordinary houses can also have an asymmetrical slight upward curve.

lm.name: Minahasa Houses
lm.note: The houses of the Minahasa people are the most distinctive architectural feature of North Sulawesi, constructed entirely of light orange-brown wood and featuring a unique roof shape with triangular elements similar to stacked Bangla roofs. The classic Minahasa house is a two-storey building on stilts, although single-storey houses also exist.

lm.name: Muna Buton Horizontally Painted Fences
lm.note: Sula fences painted red-and white horizontally, on the other hand, are common on Buton Island. These can also rarely be found on Muna Island.

lm.name: Muna Buton Houses
lm.note:
On Muna Island and Buton Island, you can see houses built from vertical wooden planks painted in alternating colours. Unpainted houses built from vertical planks are also generally indicative of the area, but less reliable.

Many of the houses are built on stilts. Often there are support beams connecting the stilts to the main body of the house. Some houses also have foundations.

lm.name: Muna Buton Lava Rock Walls
lm.note: Walls made of dark rough-textured lava rocks are common on Muna Island and Buton Island. You will also see lighter but similarly shaped rocks in walls on these islands.

lm.name: Muna Buton Red White Walls
lm.note: A good identifying feature of Muna Island and Buton Island is white and red walls. The posts of the wall are often topped with a rounded finial in a shape reminiscent of the dome of a mosque.

lm.name: Muna Buton Vertically Painted Fences
lm.note: Sula fences painted in alternating white and red sections are the most common type of fence on Muna Island. They can also sometimes be found along the west coast of Buton Island. Outside of these two islands, the fence variant may also occur.

lm.name: North Maluku Canopies & Stone Foundations
lm.note: Houses in North Maluku often have large canopies and visible stone foundations. Note that most houses in the province are more recently-built, so exposed cinder blocks and shiny or coloured metal roofs are common.

lm.name: North Maluku Low Concrete Walls
lm.note: Low concrete walls in various colours with vertical slots in the middle are very common in North Maluku. Sula fences can also occur, but less frequently.

lm.name: Orange Blue Fences
lm.note: In Polewali Mandar Regency, you can find Sula fences in an orange-blue colour combination.

lm.name: Selayar Island Floral Window Motifs
lm.note: Windows of modern dwellings on Selayar Island sometimes feature colourful floral decorations.

lm.name: Selayar Island Low Concrete Walls
lm.note: Sula fences and low concrete walls are common on Selayar Island. On the outskirts of the city of Bentang, you can find fences made of rows of trees.

lm.name: Simple Wooden Houses
lm.note: Simple wooden houses are very common in South East Sulawesi. These houses often have tiled roofs, vertical wooden window bars and open roof sections.

lm.name: Sornako Prefabricated Houses
lm.note: In the Sornako area of Luwu Timor Regency, you can see many prefabricated houses, often on stilts.

lm.name: Toli-Toli Blue
lm.note: Toli-Toli Regency also has a higher density of Bugis-style stilt houses than any other part of Central Sulawesi. A defining characteristic of Toli-Toli Regency is the colour blue. You will see blue utility poles, signs, entrance gates, and even the Sula fences are mostly painted blue and white.

lm.name: Tongkonan
lm.note: A Tongkonan is the traditional ancestral house of the Toraja people in South Sulawesi in Rante Pao and surrounding areas, easily recognized by its distinctive, boat-shaped saddleback roof pointing dramatically towards the sky.

lm.name: Belitung Sheet Metal Roofs
lm.note: Belitung Island, on the other hand, mainly has sheet metal roofs, which can be either a fresh silver colour or show signs of rust.

lm.name: Black Walls Bright Rocks
lm.note: Black walls with light-coloured rocks are common on Kundur Island and Karimunbesar Island.

lm.name: Block Shaped Houses
lm.note: Block shaped multi-story houses featuring shops or garages on the ground floor are frequently found in urban areas of North Sumatra and Riau.

lm.name: Boat Shaped Houses
lm.note: In addition to the palm-wood houses, there are also the well-known traditional Batak boat-shaped houses in the Lake Toba area. Most of the houses have highly recognisable criss-crossed stilts.

lm.name: Churches Property Graves
lm.note: The vast majority of the population of Nias Island are adherents of Protestant Christianity. Churches are common and graves on private property are not unusual.

lm.name: Circular Vents
lm.note: In the Riau Islands as well as in Northern Sumatra, houses often feature circular or semi-circular vents and windows with “spokes” radiating out from the centre . These are typically featured on the gable or above doors and windows. Similar windows and vents can be found elsewhere in Sumatra.

lm.name: Floral Gable Motifs
lm.note: In Jambi, Riau and also Batam and Bintan, intertwining floral patterns on house gables are common.

lm.name: Gate Pillars Bengkulu
lm.note: In Bengkulu, you will rarely find isolated pillars with a floral motif on top at property entrances.

lm.name: Gate Pillars Lampung
lm.note: Property entrances in Lampung also frequently feature rectangular stone pillars, often decorated, and a concrete kerb.

lm.name: Gate Pillars South Sumatra & Jambi
lm.note: Entrance pillars can be found In South Sumatra and Jambi, usually taking a turret shape with a rising balustrade attached.

lm.name: Jambi Gables
lm.note: In Jambi, you'll commonly find pointy saddle roofs, consisting of a steep top part and a more shallow flap. These often have simple X-shaped or hook-shaped gable horns attached.

lm.name: Kalimantan - Malay Canopies
lm.note: In the regions of Sumatra and Kalimantan that lie opposite Malaysia, many buildings have metal canopies with curved ends. These canopies are often blue or red.

lm.name: Kalimantan - Roof Decoration
lm.note:
Bargeboards consisting of a carved wooden frieze can be found throughout Bengkulu. This type of roof decoration can also be found in other parts of Indonesia, in particular in West Kalimantan and South Kalimantan.

In exceptional cases, this meta is also found in regions other than those previously mentioned.

lm.name: Karimunbesar Modern Row-Houses
lm.note: New residential areas with rows of modern houses and paved with hexagonal paving stones are common on Karimunbesar Island.

lm.name: Karo Crown Roofs
lm.note: The Batak Karo people in the north of North Sumatra province often construct houses with unique, highly ornate crowns, consisting of four-way gables topped off with buffalo head finials. Both modern and traditional varieties of this design exist.

lm.name: Lampung Javanese Tiles
lm.note:
Historic migration from Java has left a mark on architecture in Lampung.

Traditional Javanese tiles are common here, however the population density in Lampung is much lower, resulting in larger plots of land and widely spaced houses.

Lampung roofs often have tiles of different shades, from light orange to dark brown. There are also more houses built of wood in Lampung.

lm.name: Limas Roofs
lm.note: Limas houses are found in a narrow area in the Musi Banyuasin Regency. A characteristic feature of this house type is a top section that gradually descends forming a long street-facing extension.

lm.name: Long Bamboo Fences
lm.note:
Conspicuously long bamboo fences, usually laid horizontally, are commonly used to demarcate properties within villages in Bengkulu, and are also frequently found in rural areas. Vertically oriented bamboo fences are also common.

In addition loose piles of stones are common too. Combined with the moss gardens and long bamboo fences this can be a good indication of the province.

lm.name: Low Stilt Houses
lm.note: In coastal areas of north-east Sumatra (mainly Riau and Jambi), you can find low-stilt houses. In the north they are usually elevated by concrete frustums while wooden stilts are found further south.

lm.name: Mandailing Roofs
lm.note: In Mandailing Natal Regency, you will find houses with ornate gables and strikingly long gabled horns on large roofs. These are called Bagas Godang Panyabungan Tonga and are associated with the Batak Mandailing people.

lm.name: Metal Gable Ends
lm.note: In Bengkulu, houses often have clean corrugated metal gables, often coloured crimson or blue.

lm.name: Mosques Aceh
lm.note: Aceh is a uniquely autonomous province and the only one where Sharia Law is officially applied. Mosques are, therefore, more common, large and ornate in this region than other parts of Indonesia.

lm.name: Multi-Layered Gables With Notches
lm.note: Gables in Bengkulu are also frequently multi-layered, with notches or semi-circle patterns in the top layer. Similar notches specifically can rarely occur in other regions such as North Kalimantan and West Sulawesi.

lm.name: Nias Chief Houses
lm.note: The Omo Sebua Chief’s House, built on pillars with towering thatched roofs (or sheet metal roofs in modern versions), is characteristic of Nias Island. It is particularly common in the southern half of the island.

lm.name: Nias Flap Roofs
lm.note: Everyday houses with roofs that curve outwards to the side can be found as detached houses or in rows of houses in the southern half of Nias Island. The roof shape is a partial imitation of the Chief's House.

lm.name: Nias Gable Window Houses
lm.note: On Nias Island, you will commonly find houses that have windows in the gable end with wooden shutters that swing open.

lm.name: Nias Rounded Houses
lm.note: In the northern half of Nias Island, chieftain houses found have roofs with a significantly more rounded shape.

lm.name: Nias Thatched Roofs
lm.note: Another widespread type of house on Nias Island is simple houses built from wooden planks and equipped with thatched roofs and thatched canopies over the front. The same combination of thatched roofs and canopies can also be found on other islands in Indonesia, but usually in different shapes.

lm.name: Palembang Swamp Stilt Houses
lm.note: The area south of Palembang is full of swamps. Stilt houses with hip metal roofs are common here.

lm.name: Red Bricks Narrow
lm.note:
Red bricks are very common in Sumatra and are helpful in regionguessing or excluding specific parts of the island. They occur in two variants: narrow and wide.

Narrow red bricks are found in the northern and southern parts of Sumatra, as well as all along the west coast.

lm.name: Red Bricks Wide
lm.note:
Red bricks are very common in Sumatra and are helpful in regionguessing or excluding specific parts of the island. They occur in two variants: narrow and wide.

Wide red bricks are found in the centre-south, primarily in South Sumatra and Jambi.

lm.name: Red Stone Walls
lm.note: Low walls made of these dark red stones can be found along property borders, mostly in the south of Bintan Island, as well as very rarely on Batam Island.

lm.name: Ridge Tiles Grey
lm.note: Roofs similar to those found in Bangka Island are very common in the Riau Islands. These roofs typically consist of fibre cement sheets with grey tiles lining the edges.

lm.name: Ridge Tiles Red
lm.note: Red tiles along the edges of fibre cement roofs make houses on Bangka Island easily recognisable. Fully tiled roofs are also common.

lm.name: Rising Roofs
lm.note: Smaller structures in North Sumatra will often feature a variation of the gable design with a jagged boat roof, as opposed to the smoother curve. The rising section can be found on one or both ends of the roof.

lm.name: Siger Crown Symbol
lm.note: The Siger crown is a symbol of Lampung. Its design features a curved shape with seven or nine peaks. It can be found on gates, lamps, bridge stones, street signs and in other places.

lm.name: Spired Roofs
lm.note: In West Sumatra, you will often find houses with a boat-shaped roof—frequently multi-tiered—featuring soaring spires at the gable ends, giving them a majestic appearance.

lm.name: Stone Lamps
lm.note: Stone lamps are common at entrances in Lampung as well as in adjacent parts of South Sumatra.

lm.name: Sumatra Roofs Sheet Metal
lm.note: South Sumatra houses with sheet metal roofs (often with a dark rust-brown tone) are found in the interior, mountainous parts of the province, and can be found also in western Jambi.

lm.name: Sumatra Roofs Tiled
lm.note:
South Sumatra has very unique houses which typically consist of a top floor with many windows, serving as the main floor, built on top of a lower section which may sometimes just consist of stilts or pillars. A staircase leads to the top section. The whole house is built of timber.

Combined with a hip roof made of traditional tiles, this type of house is very recognisable.

lm.name: Bollards
lm.note:
• Indonesia commonly uses these black-and-white square or circular bollards, as well as these yellow-and-black ones, which can also have a red reflector.
  • Other designs can also be found.

--- NOTE:

  • UK-style bollards are mostly found in Kalimantan.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: License Plates
lm.note:
• Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters.
  • The letters usually appear as three white sections through the blur.
  • Plates in newer coverage can be white too.

--- NOTE:

  • Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Motorcycle Front Plates
lm.note: • Motorcycles in Indonesia have front licence plates, as opposed to other south-east Asian countries which do not.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Poles
lm.note:
• Poles in Indonesia are typically round and made out of either steel or concrete.
  • Many of the steel poles are painted black, and also feature the Indonesian flag colours on them.
  • The pole tops are usually either even or uneven, depending on the region.

lm.map: A Learnable World - Identify Every Country
lm.name: Roadlines
lm.note:
• Indonesia uses white or yellow centre lines.
  • Outer lines will always be white.
  • The centre lines will be solid or dashed.

--- NOTE:

  • In Generation 3 coverage, yellow centre lines are more rare, as Indonesia only recently started using this colour for its road lines.
