lm.name: Arrow-Shaped Extensions
lm.note: Roofs featuring an arrow-shaped extension protruding upwards are common in the eastern half of Java.

lm.name: Balinese-Style Ornaments
lm.note: These distinctive Balinese-style roof ornaments, consisting of long flat wing shapes with curled ends can be found in the far eastern end of Java.

lm.name: Bangka Style Roof
lm.note: Roofs similar to those found on Bangka Island are very common. These typically consist of fibre cement sheets and reddish tiles lining the edges. The second type of roof that is also frequently found is the fully tiled Javanese roof.

lm.name: Bawean Island Landscape
lm.note: Bawean Island is a small island quite far off the northern coast of East Java. Administratively it is part of Gresik Regency. The landscape is characterised by arid fields amidst medium-sized, vegetated mountains.

lm.name: Bawean Island Modern Lamps
lm.note: These easily recognisable, modern-looking white streetlamps can be found all over the island.

lm.name: Bromo-Tengger National Park
lm.note: Bromo-Tengger National Park possesses some of the most iconic landscapes of Indonesia. There you will find majestic terraces dotted by she-oaks and traditional villages. A few roads have coverage looking down upon the Tengger crater and Gunung Bromo.

lm.name: Candi Bentar
lm.note: Candi Bentar or “split gates” appear like a single structure split into two and are vestiges of Hinduism on Java. The sides facing each other are plain while the outsides may be highly ornate. They may be red brick or painted. They can be found at historic sites across Java but are most common in East Java.

lm.name: Concrete Strips Road
lm.note: This distinctive road type, characterised by two strips of concrete, is highly typical in Central Java, especially in the areas surrounding Surakarta and Klaten. While its presence extends into adjacent parts of West and East Java, Central Java remains the region where it is most frequently encountered.

lm.name: Corn & Teak Hills
lm.note: The region stretching from Semarang in Central Java to Ngimbang in East Java is defined by undulating hills of cornfields and teak plantations.

lm.name: Curled Metal Sheets
lm.note: Thin metal sheets with curled ends spanning the roof ridges are a common sight across most of eastern Central Java. They also frequently feature a central ornament displaying the year of construction.

lm.name: Decorative Entrance Pillars
lm.note: Roads flanked by these standalone decorative entrance pillars are common in East Java, eastern Central Java, and Yogyakarta. These may mark the entrance to a property or village.

lm.name: Dhurung Bawean
lm.note: Dhurung Bawean is a traditional architectural structure on the Indonesian island of Bawean, which serves as a lumbung (storehouse) for harvests and as an outdoor gathering place for social activities and guests. It is characterised by an unusually large roof structure supported by wooden pillars.

lm.name: Double-Pitched-Roof
lm.note: Java, particularly the eastern part of the island, features several prominent traditional architectural styles. The most notable types are the Joglo, Limasan, and Double-Pitched-Roof types. The simplest of the three roof types is the Double-Pitched-Roof. It is characterised by a multi-angled roof structure, but with only two different roof angles. Each roof surface is parallel to the long side of the house.

lm.name: Flexible Roof Sheets
lm.note: Flexible roof sheets are very common around Pulosari and Watoekoempoel in western Central Java, as well as in the villages south of Mount Lawu in the far eastern part of the province.

lm.name: Gunung Lavu
lm.note: Gunung Lavu (Mount Lawu) is probably the most useful volcano on Java Island. It is somewhat isolated and surrounded by flat fields from three directions, making it recognisable in clear weather. It is located on the border between Central and East Java.

lm.name: Heavy Agriculture & Dragonfruit
lm.note: Around south-eastern East Java is a flat landscape characterised by heavy agriculture with lots of crops, most uniquely dragon fruit. The roads are straight and grid-like and you can often see mountains to the west.

lm.name: Hindu Shrines
lm.note:
The area around Mount Bromo, especially along its northern face surrounding Wonokitri, is home to the Tenggerese - the last Hindu-majority people in Java.

The region features many Hindu design elements, the most distinct being these small shrines (Pelinggih) which are often found at intersections or in front of homes.

The region can be differentiated from Bali by the very mountainous setting with lots of mountain casuarina (she-oak) trees.

lm.name: Industrial Parks
lm.note: A lot of industrial parks can be found near the outskirts of Jakarta Metropolitan Area.

lm.name: Jakarta Narrow Alleys
lm.note: Jakarta has many narrow alleys where pedestrians, motorcycles and cars travel. Sometimes you can see skyscrapers in the distance.

lm.name: Jepara, Kudus and Pati Ornaments
lm.note: Small tooth-like embellishments and filigree motifs along the ridge and edges of the roof are common in the regencies of Jepara, Kudus and Pati. Rare examples also exist further south.

lm.name: Joglo
lm.note: Java, particularly the eastern part of the island, features several prominent traditional architectural styles. The most notable types are the Joglo, Limasan, and Double-Pitched-Roof types. Joglo houses feature a steep ‘hat’ shaped roof surrounded by large flaps on all four sides.

lm.name: Joglo Bocokan
lm.note: Rembang Regency is home to a unique traditional house known as the Joglo Bocokan. It is characterised by a Joglo base with gables on the sides, as opposed to slopes. A small transverse roof may or may not be present inside the gable.

lm.name: Koemendoeng Sugar Cane
lm.note: Around Koemendoeng, there are extensive sugarcane fields, often arranged in a grid-like pattern reminiscent of Brazilian sugarcane landscapes. Sugarcane is otherwise extremely rare in West Java.

lm.name: Leuit
lm.note: In the southeastern mountainous part of Banten, traditional Sundanese rice barns known as Leuit are still common.

lm.name: Limasan
lm.note: Java, particularly the eastern part of the island, features several prominent traditional architectural styles. The most notable types are the Joglo, Limasan, and Double-Pitched-Roof types. Limasan roofs also have a multi-angled roof structure, but unlike Joglo roofs, they are shallower and the flap is only present on two sides.

lm.name: Limestone Bricks & Grey Mortar
lm.note: Limestone bricks are common in northern East Java, including Madura Island, reflecting the limestone geology of the area. The bricks are put together with thick grey mortar, creating a striking visual distinction.

lm.name: Madura Exposed Limestone
lm.note: In some areas of Madura Island, exposed limestone rocks protrude from the dry ground.

lm.name: Madura Gently Rolling Hills
lm.note: Most of Madura Island's landscape is dominated by gently rolling hills, sometimes resembling terraces, giving these hills a patchy look. In general the landscape here is quite dry.

lm.name: Madura Reddish Soil
lm.note: Especially towards the east of Madura island, the soil becomes darker and more reddish.

lm.name: Madura Terraced Slopes
lm.note: Some terrace slopes made out of limestone rock can be found on Madura Island. These terrace slopes look very similar to those found near Yogyakarta, but in a noticeably drier landscape.

lm.name: Metal Eaves
lm.note: Metal eaves installed along the edges of the roof are highly localised to the northeastern part of Central Java. Metal eaves most commonly come in the colours blue, green, or red.

lm.name: Metal Roofs
lm.note: Although Java is well-known for its tiled roofs, communities featuring heavy or predominant use of metal roofs can be found in a number of mountainous and coastal areas on Java. Notable examples include the areas surrounding Mount Slamet (Central Java) and Mount Bromo (East Java).

lm.name: Mount Lawu Ornaments
lm.note: South-west of Mount Lawu, located in eastern Central Java, metal triangles with jagged edges can be seen adorning the end of roof ridges on corrugated metal rooftops.

lm.name: Neat Hedges
lm.note: Villages located along the southern coastal plain of Central Java, particularly in the regions stretching west of Yogyakarta, are characterised by an organised layout of small rectangular properties framed by short, neatly-trimmed hedges. These settlements mostly follow a strict grid-like pattern with a noticeable absence of winding roads.

lm.name: Octagonal Ridge Ends
lm.note: Conversely, roof ridge ends with a roughly octagonal shape are common in East Java, but are very rare on the rest of the island. Note that the diagonal sides are usually curved inward, somewhat resembling a plus (“+”) shape.

lm.name: Pacitan & Trenggalek Mountains
lm.note: The mountain ranges between Pacitan and Trenggalek form one of the most topographically distinct regions of Java, with numerous jagged peaks and rocky precipices. The mountains are often covered in Sumatran pines, with small twin-track roads winding up the slopes. Near Trenggalek you can find flat paddy fields with these mountains in the background.

lm.name: Pati & Rembang Ornaments
lm.note: Highly decorated metal or concrete triangles are seen spanning the entire ridges of roofs in Pati and Rembang regencies.

lm.name: Pentagonal Ridge Ends
lm.note: The ends of roof ridges in Java have various shapes that can be helpful for narrowing down your location on the island. Roof ridge ends in a pentagonal shape are common in Banten, West Java and Central Java, but are quite rare in East Java.

lm.name: Perforated Bricks Ornaments
lm.note: In a similar area (Pati & Rembang regencies), you will find roof ridges spanned by perforated bricks.

lm.name: Potruding Ridge Ends
lm.note: In East Java, ridge ends often stick out a small distance past the end of the roof itself. This can be very subtle, but in the right lighting it can sometimes be identified by the presence of a small shadow underneath the ridge end.

lm.name: Puteran Island Red Soil
lm.note: On Puteran Island, located directly east of Madura, the soil turns a bright red colour.

lm.name: Roof Ornaments
lm.note: Diverse roof ornaments are a common sight throughout East Java as well as eastern Central Java. These roof ornaments mostly feature winged or curled shapes and animal motifs, located at the ends and peaks of roof ridges.

lm.name: Salt Evaporation Ponds
lm.note: As Madura Island is the largest salt-producing region of Indonesia, salt evaporation ponds are a common sight, especially along the south coast of the island.

lm.name: Small Stilt Houses
lm.note: Small stilt houses with Limasan roofs are often found near traditional Madurese settlements. These stilts sometimes rest on stone foundations.

lm.name: Smooth Cement Ridge
lm.note: Roof ridges made out of smooth cement are quite common on Madura, especially on Limasan-style roofs. Some roofs on Madura feature these stubby concrete spikes on each end of the rooftop.

lm.name: Stacked Roof Tiles
lm.note: Ridges featuring multiple stacked roof tiles are particularly common in the eastern part of Central Java. You will also spot this feature in some areas of East Java.

lm.name: Staggered Tiles
lm.note: Roof tiles with this staggered, alternating pattern can be found throughout Java, but are most common in East Java and adjacent parts of Central Java.

lm.name: Stone Pedestals
lm.note: Throughout Banten and the mountainous south of West Java, many houses rest on stone pedestals, leaving the natural ground beneath exposed. These stone bases provide a level foundation, compensating for the uneven terrain in rural areas.

lm.name: Surabaya Pavement
lm.note: In East Java, particularly near Surabaya, roads frequently feature a herringbone pattern formed with diagonally laid bricks. While most common here, this brick pattern is rarely found in other Javanese provinces. Surabaya pavement can also be found on Bawean Island and Madura Island.

lm.name: Tanèyan Lanjhang
lm.note: Traditional Madurese settlements, called Tanèyan Lanjhang, consist of two or more buildings arranged around a rectangular courtyard. The main building often joins two or more identical units together.

lm.name: Tea Cultivation
lm.note: Tea cultivation is a major indicator of West Java, with large plantations found throughout the mountains of southwestern West Java.

lm.name: Thatched Roofs
lm.note: Thatched roofs are a common sight throughout Banten, especially in rural regions. While they aren't unique to Banten and appear sporadically in other parts of Java, high concentrations are found only here and in a small section of West Java.

lm.name: Thick Baroque Roofs
lm.note: Various styles of thick, baroque-style ornately-decorated rooftops can be found in East Java. Ornate rooftops featuring these semicircular openings, usually disconnected at the bottom, can be found in western East Java. Ornate rooftops featuring these tripoint designs are further localised within western East Java. They often, but not always, also feature the semicircular openings noted above.

lm.name: Untidy Field Ridges
lm.note: On Madura Island, most field boundaries are untidily-kept with random small plants growing along them.

lm.name: Vertical Wooden Attachments
lm.note: Many Javanese roofs feature narrow, vertical wooden attachments at or below the end of the roof ridge. They often appear as an upward or downward pointed arrow, but can feature a wide range of designs (e.g., heart, anchor, fork). Regardless of shape, these attachments are found commonly in East Java and also appear routinely in Central Java and Yogyakarta. Note that similar designs can sometimes be found outside Java.

lm.name: White Bricks & Red Mortar
lm.note: In the eastern part of Madura Island, houses feature walls made of white bricks and thick red mortar instead of grey, reflecting the local geology.

lm.name: Yogyakarta Terraced Slopes
lm.note: Terraced slopes made of dark, jagged limestone are very common in the eastern part of the Yogyakarta region, extending into neighbouring parts of Central and East Java. The combination of limestone terraces and abundant teak trees is a distinctive feature of this region.

lm.name: Zi8gzag Wings
lm.note: Around Mount Merbabu (just north of Yogyakarta) the Mount Merbabu zi8gzag wings occur. Small, wing-like structures, almost always in a zigzag pattern, adorn the ends of roof ridges.

lm.name: Bollards
lm.note:
Indonesia commonly uses these black-and-white square or circular bollards, as well as these yellow-and-black ones, which can also have a red reflector. Other designs can also be found.

NOTE: UK-style bollards are mostly found in Kalimantan.

lm.name: Lake Toba
lm.note: The region around Lake Toba, in North Sumatra, can be recognized by mountains surrounding the lake and Samosir Island in the middle. Overcast coverage is also common for the region.

lm.name: Nusa Islands
lm.note:
The Nusas typically look drier than other regions in Indonesia. The islands get especially dry towards the east, especially in Generation 3. Vegetation tends to look less tropical, but instead more brown with a lack of leaves. Sumba Island is also the driest of the Nusas.

NOTE: While less common, other regions such as Java can look similarly dry. Make sure to look out for other clues before guessing.

lm.name: Palu Bay
lm.note: Palu Bay is a unique slightly north-west facing bay just north of Palu city, which features mountains to the west of the bay, and a flat, more urbanised landscape to the east.

lm.name: Red Soil
lm.note: Red soil can often be found on Batam and the Banga Belitung islands, located east of mainland Sumatra.

lm.name: Bali - Architecture
lm.note:
• Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism.
  • The most important thing to look for are these crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali.
  • Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too.

lm.name: Gable Horns
lm.note:
• Roofs with gable horns can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi, Riau and Central and South Kalimantan.

--- NOTE:

  • Horned roofs are often found with Bugis roofs in South Sulawesi.
  • Use this tip along with other clues to determine which region you are in.

lm.name: Java - Tiled Roofs
lm.note:
• Tiled roofs are most commonly found on the island of Java, and sometimes nearby regions such as southern Sumatra, the Lesser Sunda Islands, and South Kalimantan.

--- NOTE:

  • The tiles on roofs in South Kalimantan and Jambi look slightly different.
  • The tiles are usually less rounded but flatter.

lm.name: Kalimantan - Wooden Chips
lm.note: • On Kalimantan, you can find these unique roofs made out of wooden chips.

lm.name: North - Plain Sheet Metal Roofs
lm.note:
• Plain sheet metal roofs are more commonly found toward the north, where tiled roofs are not found.
  • They are most commonly found on Kalimantan, Sulawesi and Sumatra.

lm.name: Churches
lm.note: • Indonesia is religiously a Muslim majority country, so seeing churches, and other Christian signs, is a good clue for these regions.

lm.name: North Sumatra - Boat Roofs
lm.note:
• North Sumatra features similarly distinct boat-shaped roofs, however the roofs are less angled upward and they do not feature spires.

--- NOTE:

  • These roofs are most commonly found near Lake Toba, due to its sacred history.

lm.name: Rante Pao - Tongkonan
lm.note:
• A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs.
  • The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.

lm.name: South Sulawesi - Slots Inside Triangles
lm.note:
• These horizontal slots inside the triangles of the roofs are almost unique to Southern Sulawesi.

--- NOTE:

  • They can rarely be found in East Kalimantan and West Nusa.

lm.name: Sumba - High-Pitched Peaks
lm.note: • You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.

lm.name: West Sumatra - Boat Roofs
lm.note: • West Sumatra features these distinct boat-shaped roofs.

lm.name: Bali black cab
lm.note: A car with a big black cab and an open back in which a variety of people ride is found in eastern Bali, south of Mount Agung

lm.name: Bali vampire hunter car
lm.note: A car with black railings and (usually) a big wooden stake lying in the bed can be found in eastern Bali, south of Mount Agung

lm.name: Architecture in Bali
lm.note: Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism. The most important thing to look for are these crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali. Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too. Andesite, a dark, volcanic rock, is a common building material in Bali. You can often see gates, walls, and other intricately carved ornaments built from this material.

lm.name: Blue Green
lm.note: You can often see thin, black poles next to regular poles near the East Peninsula of Central Sulawesi. Two pieces of tape can be seen near the top of the poles, usually light blue and green. These can rarely be seen in northern South East Sulawesi.

lm.name: Boat Shaped Roofs North Sumatra
lm.note: North Sumatra features similarly distinct boat-shaped roofs, however the roofs are less angled upward and they do not feature spires. *These roofs are most commonly found near Lake Toba, due to its sacred history.

lm.name: Boat Shaped Roofs West Sumatra
lm.note: West Sumatra features these distinct boat-shaped roofs.

lm.name: Central Sula Bollards
lm.note: Central Sulawesi features these unique bollards that are painted black on the bottom, white in the middle, and yellow on the top.

lm.name: Extra Attachment
lm.note: Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.

lm.name: Extra Support
lm.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.

lm.name: Gable Horns Roofs
lm.note: Roofs with gable horns can be found most commonly in South Sulawesi, Riau and Central and South Kalimantan. *Horned roofs are often found with Bugis roofs in South Sulawesi. Use this tip along with other clues to determine which region you are in.

lm.name: Green Paint Bridges
lm.note: Green paint can often be seen on the side of bridges in South and Central Kalimantan.

lm.name: High Peatched Peaks
lm.note: You can find these distinct roofs with uniquely high-pitched peaks on Sumba.

lm.name: Horizontal Slots
lm.note: These horizontal slots inside the triangles of the roofs are almost unique to Southern Sulawesi. *They can rarely be found in East Kalimantan and West Nusa.

lm.name: Painted Fences
lm.note: These painted fences are typically found on Sulawesi. They will be mostly painted white with blue or red.

lm.name: Rectangle
lm.note: Bali features both even and uneven poles, as well as the Lesser Sunda island variants. You can also find this unique rectangle attachment on the pole tops in Bali.

lm.name: Red Soil
lm.note: Red soil can often be found on Batam and the Bangka Belitung islands, located east of mainland Sumatra.

lm.name: Savannah
lm.note: This savannah landscape is occasionally seen on North Sumba. *In Generation 3, you will always see a white car.

lm.name: Tongkonan
lm.note: A small region of South Sulawesi, around the city of Rante Pao, features these very unique houses, called Tongkonan, that have saddle-shaped roofs. The houses themselves are also elevated from the ground.

lm.name: Triangle
lm.note: You can find these poles with a triangle attachment under the horizontal bar in the following regions. *This does not apply to stacked poles.

lm.name: Trident
lm.note: Trident style pole tops are most commonly found in Central Java and Yogyakarta, and rarely in South and West Kalimantan, and North Sumatra and Riau.

lm.name: Uneven
lm.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.

lm.name: Wooden Roofs
lm.note: On Kalimantan, you can find these unique roofs made out of wooden chips.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Nusa pole
lm.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra long support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.

lm.map: A Learnable Meta World - Poles - Beginner
lm.name: Red-white pole paint
lm.note: Many of the steel poles in Indonesia are painted black, and often feature the Indonesian flag colours on them (red and white).

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Alor Rock Wall
lm.note: Long rock walls are common on Alor. However unlike those on Rote, these walls are not made from limestone, so the stones are smoother, like large pebbles.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Bali Flat Farmlands
lm.note: Bali’s flat, expansive farmlands are primarily located in Jembrana and Tabanan regencies in the centre and southwest of the island.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Balinese Ornamental Plants
lm.note: Balinese residents have a strong tradition of cultivating ornamental plants around their homes and along public roads. Consequently, streets are frequently lined with flora such as Cordyline, Frangipani, Hibiscus, Bougainvillea, and the False Areca Palm.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Balinese Roof Ornaments
lm.note: Roof ornaments are a staple of Balinese architecture. Common features include crown-like decorations and wing-like finials at the roof ridge ends, often combined with a central element. These designs are also present in western Lombok and in neighbouring East Java, which have large Balinese populations

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Balinese Script
lm.note: Balinese employs a unique writing system derived from the Brahmi script family. Its characters are ornate and feature intricate, flowing curves, making them visually distinctive. However, with the widespread adoption of the national language, Indonesian, the traditional script is now rarely used in daily life

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Balinese Stone Wall
lm.note: In Bali, properties are typically enclosed by high stone walls, often adorned with basalt ornamentation.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Bamboo and Brick Architecture
lm.note: Houses on Alor often have a lower section made of brick and an upper section made of woven bamboo matting.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Bamboo House
lm.note: Houses made entirely of bamboo materials with sheet metal roofs are also frequently found on Sumba.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Blue Sticker
lm.note: In rare cases, blue pole stickers similar to those on Bali or Lombok are visible on Sumbawa.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Candi Bentar Gates
lm.note: These beautifully carved split gates, known as Candi Bentar, are a quintessential element of Balinese Hindu architecture. On Bali, they are predominantly crafted from dark, volcanic basalt. While they typically mark property entrances, they occasionally appear on public roads as well.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Corn on Sumba
lm.note: In western Sumba, corn is often cultivated on a large scale.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Dark Volcanic Boulders
lm.note: The eastern slopes of Mount Rinjani in Lombok can be identified by dark volcanic boulders and grey ash.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Denpasar Area
lm.note: Located in the south, Denpasar is the capital and largest city of the province. Significantly more urbanised than the rest of the island, it features bustling commercial districts and established residential neighbourhoods. Reflecting the thriving tourism industry, commercial signage is frequently multilingual.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Eastern Alor Red Soil
lm.note: Roads in the eastern part of Alor are surrounded by gentle hills of red soil.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Ende Bay
lm.note: The bay near Pulau Ende on Flores is one of the most recognisable bodies of water in Indonesia. It is sandwiched between tall mountains to the west and the majestic Gunung Meja and Iya to the east, with Pulau Ende sitting in the middle.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Flores Hat Roof
lm.note: Roofs shaped like hats are common in central Flores in areas that are ethnically Ngada, Nage and Ende. There is a very high concentration in the ethnically Ngada area around Bajawa where the houses also have distinct ornaments on both ends of the top beam.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Komodo Architecture
lm.note: Inhabitants of Komodo Island are descendants of Bugis from Sulawesi and of former convicts who were abandoned on the island. Buginese architecture therefore dominates, with triangular gables and gable horns. Green and blue are the most common colours, and houses are often built on stilts. Property boundaries are sometimes marked with loose rocks.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Komodo Blue Street Sign
lm.note: Blue street signs with an unusual font are common on Komodo Island.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Komodo Hills
lm.note: Komodo Island lies between the larger neighbouring islands of Sumbawa to the west and Flores to the east. Mountains surrounding Komodo Town are bare and covered with small trees.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Lewotolo Volcano
lm.note: Situated on the northern shore of Lembata, the Lewotolo volcano can be recognised by a heavy layer of white volcanic ash near its peak. The volcano is becoming increasingly active over the years and you can see volcanic ash erupting from its summit.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Limestone and Monsoon Landscape
lm.note: The peninsula south of Denpasar is characterised by arid monsoon forests. The terrain consists largely of white, powdery limestone. Roads are frequently cut directly into this rock, resulting in steep limestone embankments that flank the streets.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Lombok Agriculture
lm.note: Field boundaries in Lombok are wide and feature neatly cut grass, as well as small trees or other crops, distinguishing them from similar landscapes in Java.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Lombok Architecture
lm.note: Apart from ordinary Javanese tiles, roofs made of grey tiles are almost exclusive to Lombok. Another feature of Lombok architecture is the grey concrete block walls that surround properties.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Lombok Curved Roof
lm.note: This curved roof shape in Lombok is influenced by the traditional rice barns of the Sasak tribe. Whilst rice barns in their traditional form are rare, their influence can be seen in the shapes of houses, gates and shelters throughout Lombok.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Lush Eastern Bali
lm.note: The inland region of Karangasem Regency, located in eastern Bali, consists of steep volcanic hillsides cloaked in dense, lush rainforests and thick tropical vegetation, giving the area a dark green appearance.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Manggarai Conical House
lm.note: Western Flores is inhabited by the Manggarai people and their villages are usually centred around a traditional chieftain's house with a conical roof and a distinctive finial.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Matcha-Green Gras Hills
lm.note: Hills covered in matcha-green grass stretch from central Sumba towards the east coast. Trees are very rare and, when present, only cover parts of the hills. The further east you go, the more common this type of hilly landscape becomes.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Mesh Window Coverings
lm.note: Windows with bamboo mesh coverings are also a distinctive feature of houses on Alor.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Mountainous Central Bali
lm.note: Central Bali is a mountainous region, famous for its fruit cultivation. The rugged terrain is often shrouded in mist, creating a cool climate where coniferous and eucalyptus forests thrive. Several crater lakes add to the scenic beauty of this area.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: North of Denpasar Area
lm.note: Extending north from Denpasar, the land slopes gradually upwards to the volcanic peaks. This area is dominated by residential compounds and rice terraces.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Palmyra Palms on Bali
lm.note: Palmyra palms are predominantly found in the north-east part of the island.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Palmyra Palms on Sumba
lm.note: On the east coast of Sumba, you can find Palmyra palms.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Papaya along Property Boundaries
lm.note: Papaya trees along property boundaries are often visible on Timor.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Penida Terraced Rock Walls
lm.note: Limestone walls and terraced slopes are ubiquitous on Penida, whereas they are non-existent on Bali.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Penjor Bamboo Pole
lm.note: A Penjor is an elaborately decorated, long bamboo pole that serves as an important ritual object in Balinese Hinduism.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Pyrimidical Pavilion on Stils
lm.note: These pavilions on stilts with a pyramidal roof can be found throughout Lombok and Sumbawa.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Red Brick
lm.note: Red brick houses are widespread on the Nusa islands of Sumbawa and Alor. They also occur on Lombok, Flores, Lembata and Adonara, but less frequently.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Remote Western Bali
lm.note: Jembrana Regency in the west is more remote, with a lower population density. Roads are lined by dense, wild greenery rather than continuous construction and the area feels much more spacious and less enclosed. A defining feature of this region is the mown grass verges flanking the roads.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Rice Terraces
lm.note: In western Flores you can also find rice terraces in a mountainous setting. Rice terraces in such a setting are not found on other islands in the Nusas.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Rote Landscape
lm.note: Palmyra palms, banana plants and Bellyache bush are a familiar sight on Rote. Bellyache bush can be recognised by its green and purple leaves.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Rote Palm Stalk Fence
lm.note: Fences made from palm stalks in a tight wicker-weave pattern are common on Rote.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Rote Rock Wall
lm.note: On Rote, plots of land and fields are surrounded by distinctive long walls made from piled-up stones.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Ruteng Valley
lm.note: The Ruteng valley in western Flores is marked by a series of volcanoes forming a wall to its south.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Savannah Landscape
lm.note: The north-east coast of Sumba is the most arid part of the whole country, with a highly distinctive savannah landscape with few trees.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sembalun Caldera Village
lm.note: The high altitude village of Sembalun sits in a valley between the rugged green mountains of the Rinjani caldera. The landscape is easily recognisable due to the barren and treeless slopes.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sheet Metal Fence
lm.note: On Sumbawa, you will find an unusually high number of sheet metal fences compared to the rest of Indonesia. Fences and gates made of bamboo are also common.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Square Pavement
lm.note: Roads or walkways paved with dark, square paving stones are ubiquitous on Bali. These blocks are typically laid in either a straight grid or a diagonal diamond pattern.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sumba Christian Graves
lm.note: Graves on the predominantly Christian Sumba are often in the shape of a rectangular frustum with a flat table-like top.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sumba Limestone Formations
lm.note: Sumba has exposed limestone formations, particularly in the northern coastal areas. These were formed from ancient coral reefs. Deeper inland, they may contrast with reddish soil.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sumba Thatched Roof
lm.note: On the western tip of Sumba you can find these types of traditional houses with thatched roofs. The white brick houses typical of the Nusas are also found all over Sumba.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sumbawa Landscape
lm.note: Most roads on Sumbawa are on very flat terrain. However the island has lots of mountains that are always visible from these plains. Flores in contrast is entirely hilly.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sumbawa Roofs
lm.note: Sumbawa marks the boundary of the transition from tiled roofs to sheet metal roofs. While a mix of both can be found on the island’s west side, the east side is dominated by sheet metal roofing.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Sumbawa Tree Fence
lm.note: In rural Sumbawa, fields are separated from the road by rows of trees which are often pollarded. These are similar to the rows of trees that can be seen in Colombia.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Tedung Umbrella
lm.note: Tedung are tall, slender ceremonial umbrellas decorated with hanging tassels or fringes. They usually appear in bright yellow, white, red or a black-and-white checkered pattern. They are typically found standing next to shrines or temple gates; however, they can also be found in other settings.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Tiled Buginese House
lm.note: A good indicator for Sumbawa is tiled Buginese houses. These are recognisable by their tiled horizontal roof flap across the gable. The tiles are often the same style that is found on Java. This style of tile is not found on Sulawesi. These houses also typically lack balconies and are surrounded by fences.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Timber Frame House
lm.note: The most distinctive house types on Timor feature a boxy timber frame central section infilled with palm or bamboo. This type of house may also rarely be found on Rote.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Timor Speckled Ditch
lm.note: Within the Nusas there is a special type of roadside drainage ditch, that occurs commonly on Timor and to a lesser extent on Flores and Alor. This special ditch type is characterized by its dark mortar, flecked with white stones.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Timor Thatched Roof
lm.note: Traditional bamboo houses with thatched roofs are found scattered across Timor. These houses sometimes have a circular shape. Modern versions with metal roofs can also be found. Unlike Manggarai chieftain houses, these often have a short ridge with two small horns along the top.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Timor Tree Fence
lm.note: Fences made out of trees, some pollarded, and fences made from horizontally-stacked sticks are found along road sides on Timor and Rote.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Traditional Alor High House
lm.note: Traditional houses on Alor have a characteristic arrow-tip shape, are raised on stilts and feature thatched or sheet metal roofs.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Volcanoes on Bali
lm.note: Bali is home to several volcanoes, with the two most prominent being Mount Agung in the north-east and Mount Batukaru in the centre. Mount Agung is the island’s highest peak, easily identifiable by its massive, symmetrical cone that towers over the surrounding landscape. Mount Batukaru, by contrast, consists of a complex of multiple peaks.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Western Alor Coast
lm.note: Three islands are clearly visible off the west coast of Alor. The largest of these, Pura Island, is easily recognisable.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Western Flores Landscape
lm.note: The western tip of Flores has a unique dry landscape of undulating hills. In addition, the main road passing through here is distinctive for its concrete paving and green plastic netting on the cliffy roadsides.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: Western Sumba Landscape
lm.note: The west side of Sumba meanwhile is quite humid with fields surrounded by hills and poor road quality.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Nusa Tenggara
lm.name: White Brick
lm.note: White brick houses are widespread on the Nusa islands of Timor, Rote and Sumba while red brick houses are much less common.

lm.name: Architecture - Aceh Mosques
lm.note: Aceh is a uniquely autonomous province and the only one where Sharia Law is officially applied. Mosques are, therefore, more common, large and ornate in this region than other parts of Indonesia.

lm.name: Architecture - Belitung Sheet Metal Roofs
lm.note: Belitung Island, on the other hand, mainly has sheet metal roofs, which can be either a fresh silver colour or show signs of rust.

lm.name: Architecture - Black Walls Bright Rocks
lm.note: Black walls with light-coloured rocks are common on Kundur Island and Karimunbesar Island.

lm.name: Architecture - Boat Shaped Houses
lm.note: In addition to the palm-wood houses, there are also the well-known traditional Batak boat-shaped houses in the Lake Toba area. Most of the houses have highly recognisable criss-crossed stilts.

lm.name: Architecture - Circular Vents
lm.note: In the Riau Islands as well as in Northern Sumatra, houses often feature circular or semi-circular vents and windows with “spokes” radiating out from the centre . These are typically featured on the gable or above doors and windows. Similar windows and vents can be found elsewhere in Sumatra.

lm.name: Architecture - Extended Bamboo Fences
lm.note: Conspicuously long bamboo fences, usually laid horizontally, are commonly used to demarcate properties within villages in Bengkulu, and are also frequently found in rural areas. Vertically oriented bamboo fences are also common.

lm.name: Architecture - Floral Antlers
lm.note: These gable horns with rich floral patterns that resemble antlers are found mostly in Riau and on the Riau Islands. These gable horns will often be seen accompanied by similar floral decorations on the gable itself.

lm.name: Architecture - Floral Gable Motifs
lm.note: In Jambi, Riau and also Batam and Bintan, intertwining floral patterns on house gables are common.

lm.name: Architecture - Gate Pillars Bengkulu
lm.note: In Bengkulu, you will rarely find isolated pillars with a floral motif on top at property entrances.

lm.name: Architecture - Gate Pillars Lampung
lm.note: Property entrances in Lampung also frequently feature rectangular stone pillars, often decorated, and a concrete kerb.

lm.name: Architecture - Gate Pillars South Sumatra & Jambi
lm.note: Entrance pillars can be found in South Sumatra and Jambi, usually taking a turret shape with a rising balustrade attached.

lm.name: Architecture - Hipped Rusty Roofs
lm.note: Roofs in West Sumatra are typically low, hipped, and have a dark rusty colour, often with multiple trapezoid sections.

lm.name: Architecture - Jambi Gables
lm.note: In Jambi, you'll commonly find pointy saddle roofs, consisting of a steep top part and a more shallow flap. These often have simple X-shaped or hook-shaped gable horns attached.

lm.name: Architecture - Jambi Hooks
lm.note: In Jambi, you can find gable horns consisting of two hooks with downward-pointing ends.

lm.name: Architecture - Karimunbesar Modern Row-Houses
lm.note: New residential areas with rows of modern houses and paved with hexagonal paving stones are common on Karimunbesar Island.

lm.name: Architecture - Karo Crown Roofs
lm.note: The Batak Karo people in the north of North Sumatra province often construct houses with unique, highly ornate crowns, consisting of four-way gables topped off with buffalo head finials. Both modern and traditional varieties of this design exist.

lm.name: Architecture - Lampung Tiles
lm.note:
Historic migration from Java has left a mark on architecture in Lampung.

Traditional Javanese tiles are common here, however the population density in Lampung is much lower, resulting in larger plots of land and widely spaced houses.

Lampung roofs often have tiles of different shades, from light orange to dark brown. There are also more houses built of wood in Lampung.

lm.name: Architecture - Limas Roofs
lm.note: Limas houses are found in a narrow area in the Musi Banyuasin Regency. A characteristic feature of this house type is a top section that gradually descends forming a long street-facing extension.

lm.name: Architecture - Loose Stone Piles
lm.note: Loose piles of stones are common in Bengkulu villages. Combined with the moss gardens this can be a good indication of the province.

lm.name: Architecture - Low Stilt Houses
lm.note: In coastal areas of north-east Sumatra (mainly Riau and Jambi), you can find low-stilt houses. In the north they are usually elevated by concrete frustums while wooden stilts are found further south.

lm.name: Architecture - Mandailing Roofs
lm.note: In Mandailing Natal Regency, you will find houses with ornate gables and strikingly long gabled horns on large roofs. These are called Bagas Godang Panyabungan Tonga and are associated with the Batak Mandailing people.

lm.name: Architecture - Metal Gable Ends
lm.note: In Bengkulu, houses often have clean corrugated metal gables, often coloured crimson or blue.

lm.name: Architecture - Moss-Like Lawns
lm.note: In Bengkulu you can often find front gardens covered with moss-like lawns.

lm.name: Architecture - Multi-Layered Gables With Notches
lm.note: Gables in Bengkulu are also frequently multi-layered, with notches or semi-circle patterns in the top layer. Similar notches specifically can rarely occur in other regions such as North Kalimantan and West Sulawesi.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Chief Houses
lm.note: The Omo Sebua Chief’s House, built on pillars with towering thatched roofs (or sheet metal roofs in modern versions), is characteristic of Nias Island. It is particularly common in the southern half of the island.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Churches & Property Graves
lm.note: The vast majority of the population of Nias Island are adherents of Protestant Christianity. Churches are common and graves on private property are not unusual.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Flap Roofs
lm.note: Everyday houses with roofs that curve outwards to the side can be found as detached houses or in rows of houses in the southern half of Nias Island. The roof shape is a partial imitation of the Chief's House.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Gable Windows
lm.note: On Nias Island, you will commonly find houses that have windows in the gable end with wooden shutters that swing open.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Rounded Houses
lm.note: In the northern half of Nias Island, chieftain houses found have roofs with a significantly more rounded shape.

lm.name: Architecture - Nias Thatched Roofs
lm.note: Another widespread type of house on Nias Island is simple houses built from wooden planks and equipped with thatched roofs and thatched canopies over the front. The same combination of thatched roofs and canopies can also be found on other islands in Indonesia, but usually in different shapes.

lm.name: Architecture - Palembang Silver Roofs
lm.note: The area south of Palembang is full of swamps. Stilt houses with hip metal roofs are common here.

lm.name: Architecture - Red Bricks Narrow
lm.note:
Red bricks are very common in Sumatra and are helpful in regionguessing or excluding specific parts of the island. They occur in two variants: narrow and wide.

Narrow red bricks are found in the northern and southern parts of Sumatra, as well as all along the west coast.

lm.name: Architecture - Red Bricks Wide
lm.note:
Red bricks are very common in Sumatra and are helpful in regionguessing or excluding specific parts of the island. They occur in two variants: narrow and wide.

Wide red bricks are found in the centre-south, primarily in South Sumatra and Jambi.

lm.name: Architecture - Red Stone Walls
lm.note: Low walls made of these dark red stones can be found along property borders, mostly in the south of Bintan Island, as well as very rarely on Batam Island.

lm.name: Architecture - Ridge Tiles Grey-Black
lm.note: Roofs similar to those found in Bangka Island are very common in the Riau Islands. These roofs typically consist of fibre cement sheets with grey tiles lining the edges.

lm.name: Architecture - Ridge Tiles Red
lm.note: Red tiles along the edges of fibre cement roofs make houses on Bangka Island easily recognisable. Fully tiled roofs are also common.

lm.name: Architecture - Rising Roofs
lm.note: Smaller structures in North Sumatra will often feature a variation of the gable design with a jagged boat roof, as opposed to the smoother curve. The rising section can be found on one or both ends of the roof.

lm.name: Architecture - Spired Roofs
lm.note: In West Sumatra, you will often find houses with a boat-shaped roof—frequently multi-tiered—featuring soaring spires at the gable ends, giving them a majestic appearance.

lm.name: Architecture - Stone Lamps
lm.note: Stone lamps are common at entrances in Lampung as well as in adjacent parts of South Sumatra.

lm.name: Architecture - Sumatra Roofs Sheet Metal
lm.note: South Sumatra houses with sheet metal roofs (often with a dark rust-brown tone) are found in the interior, mountainous parts of the province, and can be found also in western Jambi.

lm.name: Architecture - Sumatra Roofs Tiled
lm.note:
South Sumatra has very unique houses which typically consist of a top floor with many windows, serving as the main floor, built on top of a lower section which may sometimes just consist of stilts or pillars. A staircase leads to the top section. The whole house is built of timber.

Combined with a hip roof made of traditional tiles, this type of house is very recognisable.

lm.name: Culture - Siger Crown Symbol
lm.note: The Siger crown is a symbol of Lampung. Its design features a curved shape with seven or nine peaks. It can be found on gates, lamps, bridge stones, street signs and in other places.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Bangka Quadpod
lm.note: Another very good identifying feature for Bangka Island is satellite dishes with metal quadpod mounts. On Belitung Island, satellite dishes are mounted on metal poles.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Batam City Plumbing Ads
lm.note: Throughout Batam city, you will find utility poles covered with small metal signs advertising plumbing services. They often feature the phrases “SEDOT WC”, “WASTAFEL”, and/or “MAMPET.” These are extremely common in Batam but can also rarely appear in Bintan.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Batam Electrical Logo
lm.note: Batam Island's electricity provider, Bright PLN, uses this orange and white logo. In addition to appearing on electricity meter boxes, this logo can be spotted from a distance on the sides of other electrical infrastructure on the island.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Bintan Electrical Boxes
lm.note:
Electrical boxes painted blue and white or blue and yellow can be used to identify Bintan Island over Batam Island.

Blue and white electrical boxes are unique to Bintan, whereas blue and yellow electrical boxes, while widespread in other parts of Indonesia, are not found on Batam Island. Note that plain beige or black electrical boxes also appear on both islands.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Bintan Street Sign
lm.note: These distinctive decorations on top of street signs are found on Bintan Island, mostly in and around Tanjung Pinang.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Dumai Rupat Street Signs
lm.note: This street sign design consisting of three sections, with an emblem and an earth logo (possibly in a different layout) is found in the coastal city of Dumai. A similar design can be found on Rupat Island.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Kilometre Markers  Black Border
lm.note: Kilometre markers with a black border can be found on the Pekanbaru-Dumai Highway, which cuts across hills of dense oil palm plantations. Note the southernmost section of road does not use this design.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Kilometre Markers "S"
lm.note: This highway in North Sumatra shown on the map can be recognised by the additional "S" on the right-hand side of kilometre markers.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Kilometre Markers Mounted
lm.note: The Kisaran-Indrapura Highway has kilometre markers mounted on on bent rods jutting out into the central reservation.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Lampung Pavement
lm.note: Lampung pavement typically consists of random, irregular rocks of uneven sizes, often paired with reddish soil.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Lampung Sticks
lm.note: Medium-sized sticks frequently serve as bollards along streets in Lampung. They can rarely be found elsewhere. Red and white sticks are common for these bollards but the colour may vary.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Minas Oil Field
lm.note: Situated in a hilly landscape, Minas oil field is currently the largest oil field in Indonesia. Numerous unpaved paths with oil pipelines running alongside them cross dense oil palm plantations in this area.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Oil Industry
lm.note: Oil wells are mainly found in the heavily industrial province of Riau. As a result you will often find gas pipelines, oil pumps, and oil tankers here.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Red Pole Spikes
lm.note: Dark red pole spikes are specific to Bintan Island.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Urban Aceh
lm.note:
The northeastern part of Aceh around Langsa appears quite urban with a lot of road traffic.

Poles have three or four crossbars which is unusual for Indonesia.

Boxy tuk-tuks can be seen in Langsa but can also rarely be found elsewhere in Aceh.

lm.name: Infrastructure - Yellow Numbers Black Background
lm.note: Pipelines in Riau can also help narrow down the location. For example, this pipe with ring-like sections and yellow numbers in the format 'XX.XXX' on a black background can be seen on the stretch of road shown on the map.

lm.name: Landscape - Aceh Valley
lm.note: In central Aceh, there is coverage in a long, NW-SE oriented valley coming from north Sumatra. The landscape resembles that of Lake Toba, with high mountains visible to the side of the valley.

lm.name: Landscape - Barren Tree Mountains
lm.note: The landscape around Lake Toba is unique, featuring grass-covered mountains dotted with trees. Due to its higher elevation, the clouds sometimes appear quite low.

lm.name: Landscape - Batam Bintan Red Soil
lm.note: Soil will usually be red on both Batam Island and Bintan Island.

lm.name: Landscape - Coastal Jambi
lm.note: In coastal Jambi you can also find many canals lined with areca palms.

lm.name: Landscape - Coastal Plains
lm.note: North of Pariaman is a flat plain (uncharacteristic for the west coast), with many oil palm plantations as well as groves of coconut and areca palms.

lm.name: Landscape - Eucalyptus Plantations
lm.note: Large eucalyptus plantations define the landscape of coastal Jambi.

lm.name: Landscape - Gunung Bintan Besar
lm.note: Gunung Bintan Besar (“Mount Bintan”) is the highest point on Bintan Island and can be recognised at a considerable distance with its distinct pyramidal shape.

lm.name: Landscape - Gunung Kerinci
lm.note: To the north of the regency, you can find the magnificent Gunung Kerinci located in the middle of the Sumatran range on the border between Jambi and West Sumatra. It is surrounded by a relatively flat volcanic field, itself surrounded by non-volcanic hills. Mulch films and tea plantations can sometimes be seen.

lm.name: Landscape - Harau Valley
lm.note: The Harau Valley just north of Payakumbuh is a unique karst landscape with tall exposed rock faces, often with red soil along the bottom.

lm.name: Landscape - Kaolin Extraction
lm.note: The red soil prevalent on both islands is often mixed with white kaolin (limestone). Kaolin mining areas can be found on both Bangka Island and Belitung Island.

lm.name: Landscape - Kerinci Valley
lm.note: The Kerinci Regency is located in a NW-SE oriented valley with vast expanses of rice fields between mountains on both sides. The region contains a large number of the hip-roof houses commonly seen in the west of Sumatra. Poles here are somewhat similar to those in West Sumatra.

lm.name: Landscape - Kundur Karimunbesar Yellowish Soil
lm.note: The islands of Kundur and Karimunbesar in the Riau Islands have strikingly yellow soil, which is reflected in a local architecture featuring yellowish-grey bricks. These can be mistaken for similar bricks in the Nusas.

lm.name: Landscape - Lake Danau Maninjau
lm.note: Lake Danau Maninjau west of Bukittinggi is situated inside a large caldera (Maninjau Caldera) surrounded by tall walls of mountains from all sides. It's also a well-known tourist attraction for its distinct scenery.

lm.name: Landscape - Lake Danau Singkarak
lm.note: Lake Danau Singkarak is situated at the centre of West Sumatra, sandwiched between low NW-SE mountains on both sides.

lm.name: Landscape - Moisty West
lm.note: The towering Barisan Mountains in West Sumatra catch most of the moist air currents from the Indian Ocean, creating heavy precipitation on the eastern side of the mountains. The province therefore has some of the highest rainfall in the country, appearing moist in most of the coverage.

lm.name: Landscape - Mount Sinabung
lm.note: Mount Sinabung is located 30 km northwest of Lake Toba, in Karo Regency. The volcano is cone-shaped, active, and has erupted several times in recent years. Its summit is almost devoid of vegetation and clearly visible from the surrounding area.

lm.name: Landscape - Red Hill Plantations
lm.note: The foothills of Bengkulu are dominated by a series of undulating red-soil hills upon which lie a wave of oil palm plantations and rubber trees.

lm.name: Landscape - Rural Batam Bintan
lm.note:
Rural landscapes on Bintan Island and Batam Island are broadly similar, although rarer on Batam Island since this island is more heavily developed.

Rural roadsides are often overgrown with ferns and other low groundcover. Low to modest hills are commonly visible and roads frequently cut through the hillsides leaving exposed red dirt slopes. This is especially common south of Batam.

lm.name: Landscape - Southwestern Aceh
lm.note: Several trails in the southwestern plains of Aceh have oil palm plantations and the landscape is similar to other western coastal areas of Sumatra. In areas closer to the mountains, ferns are often seen along the sides of the roads.

lm.name: Landscape - Three Volcanoes
lm.note: The three volcanoes, Gunung Singgalang, Gunung Marapi and Gunung Sago, stand out from the central uplands of West Sumatra, and can be easily recognised in the nearby area, with Marapi being the tallest one, and Sago being rather less distinctive. Due to the moist climate of West Sumatra, they are often very shroudy.

lm.name: Vegetation - Bangka Belitung
lm.note: Bangka Island and Belitung Island often have a rural feel with trees and grass lining the road. Reeds are common and some roads appear red in colour (due to the soil).

lm.name: Vegetation - Lake Toba Agriculture
lm.note: The Lake Toba area is dominated by small-scale agriculture with small garden-like fields and tea plantations. These are often lined with various flowers, in particular Clibadium surinamense (white), Mexican sunflowers (yellow) and hibiscus (red).

lm.name: Vegetation - Sweet Potato Vines
lm.note: The sweet potato plant can be recognised by its small, green and dark purple leaves. It can be found covering large areas of ground all over Nias Island.

lm.name: Vegetation - West Basin Fields
lm.note: West Sumatra is a major rice-producing province, with fields mainly located in the basin around Payakumbuh as well as the surrounding valleys. You will also find fields south of Solok, particularly cabbage fields, typically covered with recognisable black foil.

lm.note: Architecture in Bali is unique because it was influenced by old Balinese culture and Hinduism. The most important thing to look for crown-like roof pinnacles, found everywhere in Bali. Guardian statues and slit-drum towers are common too. Andesite, a dark, volcanic rock, is a common building material in Bali. You can often see gates, walls, and other intricately carved ornaments built from this material.

lm.name: North Sumatra pole
lm.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.
