lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Dragon Snake
lm.note: In Wajo Regency you can also sometimes find gable ornaments in the shape of a snake-like dragon with a raised head.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Breaking Wave
lm.note: This roof ornament with an upward curling shape, resembling a breaking wave, is exclusive to South Sulawesi, and specifically to Wajo Regency.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Buffalo Horns
lm.note: Buffalo horn roof ornaments have a similar distribution to ‘winged’ gable horns but are notably more common in South East Sulawesi and West Sulawesi.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Crossed Bars
lm.note:
Crossed roof ornaments all along the ridge of the roof are found on Nias Island.

Please note that crossed bars can also be found elsewhere—for example, in Kalimantan on the so-called "Bubungan Tinggi" chief's house. This example involves the "rabbit ear" variant appearing multiple times on the same roof.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Dagger
lm.note: On Rote Island you can find this roof ornament, which resembles a dagger amidst two upward-curving horns.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Dayak Horns
lm.note: Recognisable by their curved shape and particularly elaborate style, these gable horns are mostly found in North Kalimantan and East Kalimantan, which have the largest Dayak populations.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Fighting Roosters
lm.note: On Selayar Island you can find gable horns consisting of crossed rooster heads, sometimes also with little figures of people alongside.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Floral Antlers
lm.note: These gable horns with rich floral patterns that resemble antlers are found mostly in Riau and on the Riau Islands. These gable horns will often be seen accompanied by similar floral decorations on the gable itself.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Gable Ornaments
lm.note: This roof ornament is characterised by its intricate foliate design and its composition of three parts: one vertical and two along the sides of the roof. It is present in West Sulawesi, as well as South Kalimantan.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Jambi Hooks
lm.note: In Jambi, you can find gable horns consisting of two hooks with downward-pointing ends.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Rabbit Ears
lm.note: These elongated and ornate ‘rabbit ear’ gable horns are found in South Kalimantan.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Spear
lm.note: On Batam and Bintan you will often see simple, modern spear-shaped roof ornaments, usually painted gold or yellow, or more rarely white. As with the Riau gable horns, they often accompany floral gable decorations.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Trident
lm.note: These ornate foliate trident-shaped gable horns are found in South Kalimantan.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Vertical Finial
lm.note: Vertical finials are largely limited to West Sulawesi. They come in a rounded and a flat version.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: Wings
lm.note: The ‘winged’ gable horn can be distinguished by its serrated lower edge. It is most common in South Sulawesi but can be found on much of the rest of Sulawesi and also in eastern Kalimantan.

lm.map: A RMRG Learnable Indonesia - Gable Horns
lm.name: X
lm.note: X-shaped horns share a similar distribution as winged gable horns, but can also sometimes be found in Jambi and on the Riau Islands.

lm.name: bali square
lm.note: Bali features both even and uneven poles, as well as the Lesser Sunda island variants. You can also find this unique rectangle attachment on the pole tops in Bali.

lm.name: blue and green markings
lm.note: You can often see thin, black poles next to regular poles near the East Peninsula of Central Sulawesi. Two pieces of tape can be seen near the top of the poles, usually light blue and green. These can rarely be seen in northern South East Sulawesi.

lm.name: even but uneven
lm.note: These poles are almost exclusive to North Sumatra. The bar which holds the insulators is even, but features uneven insulators with one on one side and two on the other.

lm.name: nusas extra support
lm.note: On the Lesser Sunda Islands (“Nusas”), you can find poles with an extra support on the pole top. Sometimes, two supports can be present.

lm.name: sulawesi extra attachment
lm.note: Pole tops in North and Central Sulawesi, and Gorontalo commonly feature an extra attachment right under the horizontal bar.

lm.name: triangle attachment
lm.note:
You can find these poles with a triangle attachment under the horizontal bar in the following regions.

NOTE: This does not apply to stacked poles.

lm.name: trident
lm.note: Trident style pole tops are most commonly found in Central Java and Yogyakarta, and rarely in South and West Kalimantan, and North Sumatra and Riau.

lm.name: Banjar Chieftains House
lm.note: In parts of South Kalimantan, you can see the traditional chieftains’ houses of the Banjar people. These are known as Rumah Bubungan Tinggi, meaning 'high peak' houses, due to their steep gable roofs. The whole house is built on top of high stilts.

lm.name: Bright Colours
lm.note: The further north-east you go in Kalimantan, the more likely you are to find houses painted in bright colours.

lm.name: Bright Yellow Theme
lm.note: In the coastal cities of West Kalimantan, especially Pontianak, you will occasionally see bright-yellow buildings and monuments. The colour dates back to the Pontianak Sultanate, where yellow signified Malay royalty, and the tradition has persisted locally.

lm.name: Buginese Features
lm.note: Simple, elevated houses built on wooden stilts with Buginese roof features can be found along the north-east coast of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Chinese Architecture
lm.note: Along the west coast of West Kalimantan, especially in the northwest and the city of Singkawang, you will notice a lot of Chinese architecture and inscriptions. As well as the distinctive paifang-style gates and klenteng (temples), there are many Chinese cemeteries with characteristic rounded, horseshoe-shaped tombs. Similar features appear across Indonesia wherever there are sizable Chinese communities, but West Kalimantan has the largest Chinese population in Indonesia.

lm.name: Coal Mining
lm.note:
Certain areas of Kalimantan are known for coal mining. These include **Samarinda **and the areas shown on the map.

Indicators of the industry include ships or yellow trucks carrying coal, visibility poles near mining sites, conveyor belts, grey-black soils and ponds full of mine tailings.

lm.name: Dark Red Soil
lm.note: The areas in Central Kalimantan shown on the map have remarkably dark red soil, in contrast to the lighter soil found elsewhere in Kalimantan.

lm.name: Dayak Architecture
lm.note:
The Dayak are the indigenous people of Borneo and generally inhabit more inland parts of the island. Malinau, Kutai Barat and Sintang regencies have the most prominent Dayak populations.

Dayak traditional art is extremely intricate and curvy and can be found painted on walls, fences, poles and other surfaces. Key motifs include the Aso (a mythical hybrid of a dog and dragon representing strength), the Hornbill (symbolising nobility and bravery), and an elongated hexagonal shield.

lm.name: East Coast Grass
lm.note: Along the east coast of East Kalimantan, the soil is noticeably light with patches of grass. North of Samarinda the soil becomes very rocky.

lm.name: Flooded Plains
lm.note: The western part of South Kalimantan is a very flat plain that is frequently flooded, with many houses built on stilts. Numerous irrigation waterways are visible, with rice cultivation being very common.

lm.name: Horizontal Boards
lm.note: Banjarese houses in South Kalimantan have wide, horizontal boards spanning the top of the front of the houses. These boards can be wooden or metal.

lm.name: Jerkinhead Roof
lm.note: Many modern houses in South Kalimantan incorporate elements of the traditional Banjarese traditional Gajah Manusu houses. In particular, they often feature its signature jerkinhead roof.

lm.name: Lampung Influence
lm.note: In the south of South Kalimantan you will find many of the same features that are associated with Lampung, including Hindu religious structures, property entrance wing walls, and sticks used as bollards.

lm.name: Lampung Style Tiled Roof
lm.note: Within Kalimantan, Lampung-style tiled roofs are found in the provinces of Central, South and East Kalimantan.

lm.name: Limestone Karst Formation
lm.note: Along the main road that runs along the north-east side of the Meratus Mountains, distinctive limestone karst formations are visible.

lm.name: Long Wooden Walkways
lm.note: Houses with long wooden walkways leading up to them from the road are more common towards North and East Kalimantan, but are found sporadically across all of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Malay Style Halls
lm.note: Monumental Malay-style halls appear occasionally in West Kalimantan. Typical features include a broad central staircase, spacious verandas and numerous tall stilts. You will also find modern variants that keep only some elements, principally the grand, columned look.

lm.name: Meratus Mountains Foothills
lm.note: In western Tanah Laut Regency, in the foothills of the Meratus Mountains, you can see unusually barren hilltops.

lm.name: Mount Kelam
lm.note: Mount Kelam is a distinctive landmark: a huge, bare, rounded massif rising from an otherwise flat plain. It is often visible from far away, especially from Sintang. The area immediately around Mount Kelam is also very recognisable with dense settlements and massive boulders very close to the houses.

lm.name: Neatly Mowed Front Gardens
lm.note: Kuta Barat Regency stands out for its very neatly mowed front gardens, which sometimes even appear slightly mossy.

lm.name: Orange Soil
lm.note: Much of East Kalimantan is covered in exposed orange soil. You often come across roads built into red rocky landscapes. Particularly orange-coloured soil can be found around Muarawahau.

lm.name: Pulau Derawan
lm.note: Pulau Derawan is a tiny island with trekker coverage located off the northern tip of East Kalimantan. It can be easily recognised by its wooden piers, white sand and colourful low-stilt houses.

lm.name: Rosette Designs
lm.note: Rosette designs on gables are fairly common in West Kalimantan. They can be seen elsewhere in Indonesia too, but within Kalimantan, they are most likely to be seen in West Kalimantan.

lm.name: Rubber Tree Plantations
lm.note: Rubber plantations are common in the western foothills of the Meratus Mountains and in the coastal area across from Laut Island. The plantations are often located along very narrow, winding roads.

lm.name: Singkawang Area
lm.note: The Singkawang area is easy to distinguish from other large cities by the sharp, towering peaks that surround it.

lm.name: Swampy + Heath Forest
lm.note: The area in Central Kalimantan shown on the map, which includes the Trans-Kalimantan route towards South Kalimantan, is a swampy region with heath forest.

lm.name: Tall Wooden Towers
lm.note: These tall wooden towers are used for farming swallows’ nests, a Chinese delicacy. Concrete versions of the structure are common across Kalimantan; however, the wooden variant is mostly only present in the eastern half of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Traditional Longhouse
lm.note: The traditional longhouse is the most iconic architectural form of the Dayak people across Kalimantan and is the core of their communal and social life. These longhouses are more common inland and in northern parts of Kalimantan.

lm.name: Vertical Panels
lm.note: Houses in the south-east of Kalimantan sometimes feature a prominent set of uniform vertical panels that serve as the main front access to the house. The panels are framed in a distinct colour creating a striking facade.

lm.name: White Sand
lm.note: In the central part of Central Kalimantan around Palangkaraya, the soil consists of very white sand.

lm.name: Wooden Shingles
lm.note: Houses with traditional wooden shingles are present in Central, South and East Kalimantan.

lm.name: Ampana Mountains & Lamps
lm.note: Ampana, the capital of Tojo Una-Una, is characterised by a "layered" mountain backdrop that is frequently shrouded in clouds. The city is also known for the long, green lamps attached to its utility poles.

lm.name: Bamboo Fences
lm.note: In addition to Sula fences, many bamboo fences can be found in the southern part of the South East Sulawesi.

lm.name: Bamboo-Lattice Pavilions
lm.note: In the southern part of South Sulawesi, including Selayar Island, you can sometimes find bamboo-lattice pavilions. These mark the entryway from the roadside to a household property and range from simple flat arches to small roofed pavilions.

lm.name: Bombana & Kolaka Regencies Landscape
lm.note: On the border between Bombana and Kolaka Regency you can find an open landscape of dry grassy rolling hills, with random crop fields and shrubs in between.

lm.name: Brick Manufacturing
lm.note: Brick manufacturing is common across Peleng Island. White bricks and sometimes the sand needed for their production, can be seen stored along the narrow roads.

lm.name: Buginese Architecture
lm.note:
Bugis houses are typically elongated wooden stilt houses elevated well above the ground.

They are topped by a simple gabled roof. The front gable often features a distinctive finial. The houses also have a gable end formed from panels and with a distinctive shape. The number of overlapping panels indicates the social status of the owner.

Access to these houses is via a steep, usually single-flight staircase leading directly to a protruding open or semi-open veranda.

lm.name: Bugis House 90° Turn
lm.note: The third type of Bugis house staircase has a 90-degree turn. This type occurs in central South Sulawesi and the southern part of West Sulawesi.

lm.name: Bugis House Parallel Staircase
lm.note: Meanwhile, Bugis houses with staircases running parallel to the road are widespread throughout Sulawesi, with the exception of Gorontalo and North Sulawesi. Their main distribution area is South Sulawesi and West Sulawesi.

lm.name: Bugis House Perpendicular Staircase
lm.note: Bugis stilt houses with the wooden staircase perpendicular to the road, as opposed to parallel to it, are much more common in the very south of mainland South Sulawesi. They also occur in the far south and north of West Sulawesi and are the dominant type of staircase on Selayar Island.

lm.name: Buol Green & Yellow Colour Scheme
lm.note: Meanwhile, Buol Regency favours a green and yellow colour scheme. You will see these colours on political posters, official buildings, fences, and monuments. However, keep in mind that the majority of Sula fences here remain mostly blue and white, similar to those in Toli-Toli Regency.

lm.name: Buton Island Landscape
lm.note: Buton Island, in contrast to Muna Island, is less arid and has comparatively green, high hills.

lm.name: Central Sulawesi Infrastructure
lm.note: The infrastructure of Central Sulawesi is quite distinctive. The province has unique bollards with a yellow-white-black colour scheme. White flaps are attached near the top of utility poles and secured by two horizontal clamps. Furthermore, spiky possum guards are a frequent sight across the region, typically mounted with a noticeable downward angle.

lm.name: Coconut Palms & Alocasia
lm.note: Most of Halmahera island is sparsely populated but densely forested by coconut palms and a wide expanse of vines and ferns underneath the canopy. Clusters of Alocasia in the wild are mainly found on Halmahera, although they are not unique to the island.

lm.name: Coconut Palms & Clove Trees
lm.note: Groups of coconut palms are frequently found in North Sulawasi in fields, on mountains and in the rainforest. Clove trees growing in groups on mountain slopes are also a common sight. The often rainforest-like landscape includes bamboo, lianas, and large-leaved taro plants in the understory.

lm.name: Dark Red Soil
lm.note: Morowali Utara Regency is identifiable by its intense, dark red soil. Around the capital of Kolonodale, this red soil is paired with striking mountain formations that make the area easy to recognise.

lm.name: Dondo Houses
lm.note: Toli-Toli Regency is the home of the Dondo people. Their traditional dwellings are very simple, rustic-looking wooden houses built on stilts. These structures are typically longer than they are wide and are built from raw, untreated wood. They also feature gable roofs and simple wooden bridges leading to the entrance.

lm.name: Dry & Scrubby Landscape
lm.note: Towards the eastern end of the Banggai peninsula, the landscape becomes very dry and scrubby, resembling the Nusa islands with thin trees, giant milkweed, and white acacia.

lm.name: Dry Hills + Sugarcane
lm.note: Dry undulating hills with sugar cane can be found in eastern Bombana Regency. Ridges may also be visible to the north and south.

lm.name: Dry, Ochre-Coloured Soil
lm.note: The region shown on the map has dry, ochre-coloured gravelly soil. The area is covered by large bamboo groves, but you can also find oil palms and teak trees.

lm.name: Dutch Colonial Architecture
lm.note: The old town area around the harbour of Donggala featured well-preserved Dutch colonial architecture. Most striking are the buildings with rounded corners, a design element rarely seen elsewhere in Indonesia.

lm.name: Earthen Cliffs
lm.note: Near the town of Mamasa, you will often see earthen cliffs with a pinkish tinge topped with Sumatran pines. In contrast, it is rare to see this type of landscape in Tana Toraja because most of the roads there go around hills instead of cutting right through them.

lm.name: Flat Rice Fields
lm.note: The area around Danau Tempe in central South Sulawesi can be recognised by flat rice fields dotted with scattered coconut palms and Palmyra palms. Mountain ranges can often be seen in the distance.

lm.name: Floral Window Motifs
lm.note: Windows of modern dwellings on Selayar Island sometimes feature colourful floral decorations.

lm.name: Gorontalo Corn & Sugarcane
lm.note: As in North Sulawesi, coconut palms are common in Gorontalo. However Gorontalo has more arable land with corn and sugarcane frequently cultivated. Fields are often surrounded by rows of tree fences.

lm.name: Gorontalo E-W Mountain Ridges
lm.note: Gorontalo has E-W mountain ridges along its north and south coasts which are often visible from the area between them.

lm.name: Gorontalo Matcha Chocolate Cake Hills
lm.note: In many parts of Gorontalo you can find the famous ‘Gorontalo Matcha Chocolate Cake Hills’. These gentle rolling hills are varying shades of green and brown with valleys in between them. You can find them in the Gorontalo and in the eastern part of Buol Regency. The area around Gorontalo City and Lake Limboto is flatter however.

lm.name: Grey Unpaved Roads
lm.note: The Banggai Peninsula features many grey unpaved roads composed of fine gravel. The southern coast of the peninsula is marked by large oil palm plantations.

lm.name: Grid Layouts & Hedges
lm.note: Many villages in South East Sulawesi have grid-like layouts and well-maintained hedges, which are often strikingly long.

lm.name: Hedges with Blooming Flowers
lm.note: Throughout Central Sulawesi, villages are characterised by neatly maintained, low-growing hedges that frequently feature blooming pink flowers.

lm.name: Hindu Architecture
lm.note: In the central southern part of South East Sulawesi, you can find a lot of Hindu-related architecture.

lm.name: Incorporated Tree Fence
lm.note: It is common in Central Sulawesi to see fences that directly incorporate tree stumps, similar to those found in Mexico.

lm.name: Karst Landscape
lm.note: Karst landscapes can be seen in the Enrekang and Tana Toraja regencies. The mountains in this area commonly feature sharp peaks and rocky edges and are significantly higher, steeper and more jagged than the karst mountains found further south in South Sulawesi.

lm.name: Kolaka Oil Palms
lm.note: Southern Kolaka Regency is home to oil palm plantations, paired with the characteristic light brown gravel of the regency.

lm.name: Kolondale Bay
lm.note: Kolonodale Bay features calm, lake-like waters with large mountains to the north and east.

lm.name: Lake Poso
lm.note: Lake Poso is located in a vast valley in inland Central Sulawesi. The lake is large enough that the opposite side is not always visible, so it can be mistaken for the sea. There are mountains rising directly from the water’s edge, with the mountains on the west side of the lake being higher. To the south of the lake lies a flat valley with gridded village layouts and various tree plantations next to rice paddies.

lm.name: Lake Tondano Patchouli
lm.note: Lake Tondano is surrounded by mountains. Near the lake there are fields where patchouli, a small plant similar to mint, is cultivated.

lm.name: Large Canopies & Stone Foundations
lm.note: Houses in North Maluku often have large canopies and visible stone foundations. Note that most houses in the province are more recently-built, so exposed cinder blocks and shiny or coloured metal roofs are common.

lm.name: Large Rocks
lm.note: Large rocks are clearly visible on some of the hills in Gorontalo.

lm.name: Lava Rocks
lm.note: Walls made of dark rough-textured lava rocks are common on Muna Island and Buton Island. You will also see lighter but similarly shaped rocks in walls on these islands.

lm.name: Limestone Cliffs
lm.note: Mountains in southern Pangkajene Dan Kepulauan Regency and northern Maros Regency can be easily recognised by their typical karst formation hills. Steep limestone cliffs can also sometimes be seen in the distance.

lm.name: Low Concrete Walls with Vertical Slots
lm.note: Low concrete walls in various colours with vertical slots in the middle are very common in North Maluku. Sula fences can also occur, but less frequently.

lm.name: Luwu Pebble Roads
lm.note: Completely flat areas in the Luwu regencies can be recognised by the extremely common pebble roads there. These often have grass growing by the sides and occasionally down the middle of the road. Even paved roads are likely to have pebbles or sometimes gravel along the sides of the road.

lm.name: Luwu Utara NW Ridge
lm.note: A ridge can sometimes be seen to the northwest in Luwu Utara Regency.

lm.name: Luwuk Curved Mountain Ridge
lm.note: Luwuk, the largest city on the Banggai peninsula, is recognisable by the long, curved ridge to the northwest. This ridge has a distinctive appearance with the mountains being a uniform height interrupted by the notches made by cols. A tall red-white telephone tower in the middle of the city can also help with identification.

lm.name: Mamasa Banua
lm.note: Banua, the traditional houses of the Mamasa people in West Sulawesi, have distinctive roofs. These are arched with curves upwards at both ends. They are usually asymmetrical, with one of the ends taller than the other. Ordinary houses can also have an asymmetrical slight upward curve.

lm.name: Mamasa Canyon
lm.note: The undulating terrain of Mamasa Canyon is characterised by exposed rock walls and a high number of pine trees in the nearby highlands.

lm.name: Mamasa NE-SW Valley
lm.note: The town of Mamasa is situated in a NE-SW valley with exceptionally high mountains to the north.

lm.name: Minahasa Houses
lm.note: The houses of the Minahasa people are the most distinctive architectural feature of North Sulawesi, constructed entirely of light orange-brown wood and featuring a unique roof shape with triangular elements similar to stacked Bangla roofs. The classic Minahasa house is a two-storey building on stilts, although single-storey houses also exist.

lm.name: Modern Sasadu House
lm.note: At the northern tip of North Maluku, modern versions of the traditional Sasadu house with a highly recognisable metal roof construction can be found. The roof shape consists of a Bangla roof with a particularly protruding gable.

lm.name: Mount Klabat
lm.note: Mount Klabat volcano rises 2,000 meters above North Sulawesi’s two major cities, Manado and Bitung. Note that North Sulawesi is the only province in Sulawesi with volcanoes.

lm.name: Mountainous Terrain
lm.note: North Sulawesi has mountainous terrain.

lm.name: Muna & Buton Houses
lm.note:
On Muna Island and Buton Island, you can see houses built from vertical wooden planks painted in alternating colours. Unpainted houses built from vertical planks are also generally indicative of the area, but less reliable.

Many of the houses are built on stilts. Often there are support beams connecting the stilts to the main body of the house. Some houses also have foundations.

lm.name: Muna & Buton Red White Walls
lm.note: A good identifying feature of Muna Island and Buton Island is white and red walls. The posts of the wall are often topped with a rounded finial in a shape reminiscent of the dome of a mosque.

lm.name: Muna Island Landscape
lm.note: Muna Island is significantly flatter than Buton Island and has many fields with an arid appearance.

lm.name: Narrow Concrete Paths
lm.note: Narrow concrete paths are common in Polewali Mandar Regency.

lm.name: Nickel Production Facilities
lm.note: The Morowali regencies are particularly unique. Morowali Regency itself is heavily defined by the massive nickel production facilities in Labota.

lm.name: Orange & Blue Fences
lm.note: In Polewali Mandar Regency, you can find Sula fences in an orange-blue colour combination.

lm.name: Organised Coconut Palm Groves
lm.note: In the north and east of the Banggai peninsula, you will find organised groves of coconut palms with clear ground apart from minimal weed growth.

lm.name: Pale Soil
lm.note: In contrast to the other parts of the Morowali regencies, the western part of North Morowali Regency features very bright, pale soil which is visible on both road shoulders and dirt tracks. It also contains the largest oil palm plantations in Central Sulawesi.

lm.name: Palu Valley
lm.note: The Palu Valley is a SE-NW valley that widens to its north. It is lined with some of the most striking mountainsides in the country. Throughout the valley, you will encounter light, almost sandy soils alongside expansive agricultural areas. Coconut palms are also very common here.

lm.name: Parigi Flat Coastal Plain
lm.note: The Parigi region features an unusually wide, flat coastal plain dominated by rice fields.

lm.name: Peleng Island & Banggai Island Landscape
lm.note: On Peleng Island and Banggai Island, it is common to see small paved paths running through a densely vegetated landscape. Ferns grow extensively on the islands and coconut trees are ubiquitous along the coasts. The presence of ferns helps to distinguish this area from North Sulawesi which also has large groves of coconut palms.

lm.name: Prefabricated Houses
lm.note: In the Sornako area of Luwu Timor Regency, you can see many prefabricated houses, often on stilts.

lm.name: Pulau Makassar & Buton Island Bridge
lm.note: Pulau Makassar and Buton Island are connected by a strikingly narrow concrete bridge with blue railings.

lm.name: Rice Fields & NE-SW mountains
lm.note: This valley in North Sulawesi is fairly recognisable with rice fields enclosed by NE-SW mountain ridges on both sides.

lm.name: Rubber Tree Forests
lm.note: South of Tinompo in Morowali Utara Regency, there are a number of small roads lined with forests of rubber trees, planted in a disorganised fashion

lm.name: Selayar Island Architecture
lm.note:
The architecture of Selayar Island is characterised by the large number of Bugis-style houses. These sometimes have thatched gables. Modern houses typically have fibre cement roofs with sheet metal lining the edges.

Note: The elements mentioned are to be understood as a combination specific to Selayar Island. Individual elements, such as fiber cement roofs with metal lining, also occur elsewhere.

lm.name: Selayar Island Vegetation
lm.note: Along with numerous coconut palms, the vegetation of Selayar Island is characterised by various bushes with distinctive blossoms: lantana bushes with small orange blossoms and teak tree blossoms. You will also see easily identifiable fan-shaped gebang palms.

lm.name: Selayar Low Concrete Walls
lm.note: Sula fences and low concrete walls are common on Selayar Island. On the outskirts of the city of Bentang, you can find fences made of rows of trees.

lm.name: Seluang Rice Fields
lm.note: The region around Seluang is the largest rice-producing area in Central Sulawesi.

lm.name: Simple Wooden Houses
lm.note: Simple wooden houses are very common in South East Sulawesi. These houses often have tiled roofs, vertical wooden window bars and open roof sections.

lm.name: Sinjai Rolling Landscape
lm.note: Sinjai Regency has a subtle rolling landscape.

lm.name: Sornako Red Soil
lm.note: The eastern part of Luwu Timur Regency near Sornako is recognisable by its distinct red soil. Roads there also have a dark red tinge. You can sometimes see the lakes Danau Matano and Danau Towuti in the distance.

lm.name: South East Sulawesi Plain
lm.note: The South East Sulawesi plain is characterised by its distinct blindingly-white chalky soil. The soil can commonly have a red or brown tinge, with fine grass growing on the side.

lm.name: South Sulawesi Hindu Gardens
lm.note: Cultural influences are also visible in the landscape; small Hindu gardens featuring statues are present throughout the province, with particular hotspots located on the Banggai Peninsula and along the coast south of Parigi.

lm.name: Southern Sulawesi Higher Altitude Regions
lm.note: Higher altitude regions in Southern Sulawesi can be recognised by a hilly yet not quite mountainous feel. Unlike in the north, roads tend to be paved with asphalt instead of concrete.The architecture in this area is usually a mix of traditional Buginese stilt houses and single-storey modern brick houses.

lm.name: Tana Toranja Terraces
lm.note: The landscape in Tana Toraja Regency consists of rice terraces surrounded by hills of scattered forests. These hills are dotted by vernacular villages with narrow concrete paths winding through hills. Bamboo and Sumatran pines are also common in this area.

lm.name: Ternate Island Landscape
lm.note: Ternate is essentially one big volcano - Gunung Gamalama. Areas with coverage are usually densely-populated with narrow, inclined roads on the foothills of the volcano.

lm.name: Tidore Island Landscape
lm.note: Tidore consists of two volcanoes: Kie Matubu, a cone-shaped volcano with a partially bald peak, in the south and a bumpy caldera volcano in the north. The island is less densely-populated than Ternate.

lm.name: Toli-Toli Blue Colour Scheme
lm.note: Toli-Toli Regency also has a higher density of Bugis-style stilt houses than any other part of Central Sulawesi. A defining characteristic of Toli-Toli Regency is the colour blue. You will see blue utility poles, signs, entrance gates, and even the Sula fences are mostly painted blue and white.

lm.name: Tongkonan House
lm.note:
As well as the traditional Tongkonan houses with saddle-shaped roofs, the area around Tana Toraja contains houses influenced by both the local traditional architecture and Buginese architecture. These commonly feature multi-layered gable roofs with a slight bulge at the end.

This roof type can also be found in two other areas: one south of Lake Matano and another east of Lake Poso in Central Sulawesi.

lm.name: Tree Trunk Bollards
lm.note: In some villages on Peleng Island, you can find bollards made from tree trunks.

lm.name: Twin Volcanoes
lm.note: Two active twin volcanoes, Mount Lokon and Mount Empung, lie south of Manado. Mount Lokon is recognisable by its conical shape, light green base colour, and dark green forests on its slopes.

lm.name: Unplastered Grey Brick
lm.note: Architecture in Central Sulawesi is defined by its simplicity. Throughout the province, simple wooden houses are very common, but the most widespread building material is unplastered grey brick, which is far more prevalent than red brick. It is common to see houses where the front facade has been painted while the sides remain exposed and unplastered.

lm.name: West Sulawesi Coastal Hills
lm.note: The coastal hills in the northern half of West Sulawesi are covered with oil palm groves, the largest area of such groves in Sulawesi. The N-S main road is paved and has grey rocky soil at its sides. Side roads are often unpaved with a grey rocky soil surface entirely. Narrow stalls selling goods are common along the main roads in this region.

lm.name: West Sulawesi Coastal Plain
lm.note: The coastal plains in southern West Sulawesi are characterised by flat farmland, often rice paddies, surrounded by mountains to the north, east and west. Small groups of coconut palms are often clearly visible in the distance. The surrounding settlements feature the Buginese-style houses typical of the region.

lm.name: Yellow & Blue Bollards
lm.note:
Yellow-and-blue bollards and fences are a strong indication of North Maluku. They are less commonly found in North Kalimantan (and extremely rare on Adonara and in East Java).

You can also see other miscellaneous items with this colour scheme in North Maluku.

Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters. The letters usually appear as three white sections through the blur.

Commercial vehicles use yellow licence plates.

Plates in newer coverage can be white too.

NOTE: Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.
top.raw: Indonesian licence plates are black with white letters. The letters usually appear as **three white sections** through the blur. Commercial vehicles use yellow licence plates. Plates in newer coverage can be [white](https://maps.app.goo.gl/41BknjygGkkbi1CJ6) too. NOTE: Malaysian licence plates are also black, but generally have two white sections.

top.html:
Indonesia drives on the left.

NOTE: Malaysia drives on the left, while the Philippines drives on the right.
top.raw: Indonesia drives on the **left**. NOTE: Malaysia drives on the left, while the Philippines drives on the right.

top.html:
Indonesia uses white or yellow centre lines. Outer lines will always be white. The centre lines will be solid or dashed.

In Generation 3 coverage, yellow centre lines are more rare, as Indonesia only recently started using this colour for its road lines.

NOTE: Malaysian road lines are always all white.

In Generation 3 coverage, yellow centre lines are more rare, as Indonesia only recently started using this colour for its road lines. NOTE: Malaysian road lines are always all white.

top.html:
Poles in Indonesia are typically round and made out of either steel or concrete. Many of the steel poles are painted black, and also feature the Indonesian flag colours on them. The pole tops are usually either even or uneven, depending on the region.

_You can learn more about regional poles in the region-guessing section._

Many of the steel poles are painted black, and also feature the **Indonesian flag colours on them**. The pole tops are usually either [even](https://goo.gl/maps/rnii3wodNEqzH2FDA) or [uneven](https://goo.gl/maps/jA77LfkLbiz5AbK37), depending on the region. _You can learn more about regional poles in the region-guessing section._

Usually yellow waystones that are angled towards the road, and have a cutout close to the top are unique to Indonesia. They include shorthand for three cities or towns, with the biggest one being on the top in the cutout section.

NOTE: Waystones in the Philippines are perpendicular to the road and have the text facing away from the road.

top.html:
Indonesian can look very similar to Malaysian, however Indonesian has been influenced by Dutch, and Malaysian by English. These small changes in spelling may help differentiate the two.

An example is the word television in English, which translates to ‘televisi’ in Indonesian, similar to the Dutch word ‘televisie.’ In Malaysian, it translates to ‘televisyen’, more similar to English.
top.raw: Indonesian can look very similar to Malaysian, however Indonesian has been influenced by **Dutch**, and Malaysian by English. These small changes in spelling may help differentiate the two. An example is the word television in English, which translates to ‘televisi’ in Indonesian, similar to the Dutch word ‘televisie.’ In Malaysian, it translates to ‘televisyen’, more similar to English.

top.html: Cigarette ads can be found all over Indonesia, usually with a black or red colour scheme and around a price of 18,000 Rp. Keep an eye out for illustrated graphic pictures, and the word ‘PERINGATAN’.
